item.title: [mlb.com] 5 reasons the Yankees can win without Judge
item.dc:creator: Bryan Hoch

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK – The news about Aaron Judge’s return to the injured list was still fresh, having been announced less than an hour earlier, and already Cody Bellinger was envisioning how the Yankees could succeed in the postseason without their captain.
Unfortunately for Judge and his club, they’ve had plenty of practice doing exactly that this season. They’ve had no choice.
“Missing Judge, it hurts,” Bellinger said. “We all know he’s the best hitter in the game. For us in here, our mindset is, we’re going to have to find a way. I think the talent in this locker room speaks for itself. I’m fully confident that we have enough talent in here to go out, win and beat anybody.”
Now they’ll have their chance to prove it.
Yankees manager Aaron Boone said Tuesday that Judge is dealing with a “moderate” strain of his right calf and is not expected to be ready for a potential American League Wild Card Series against the Red Sox, which would begin on Sept. 29.
Judge’s availability for subsequent rounds, especially the AL Division Series, is also in doubt. But the Yankees need to get there first. Here are five reasons why the Yankees, lauded as pennant favorites, still can reach the Fall Classic even if Judge doesn’t return:
Dominant starting pitching
Rodón might not even draw a start in a potential Wild Card Series, standing in line behind AL Cy Young Award frontrunner Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole and Max Fried. Simply put, the rotation has kept them afloat.
Yankees starters have permitted two earned runs or fewer in 40 of 51 starts since July 28, including one earned run or fewer in 33 of those starts, compiling a 2.50 ERA over that span. Overall, they’ve allowed one run or fewer in 65 games, a single-season franchise record.
“We come to win every game, regardless of who is on the field,” Rodón said. “Obviously it’s tough when you don’t have the best player in the world on the field with you. I’m hopeful that he’ll be back. But … it’s just about winning games for us.”
There’s other thump
This isn’t 2022, when Judge’s 62 home runs set a single-season AL record and served as the unquestioned engine of the offense. Mostly because of the rib injury, Judge was limited to a .241 average, 18 homers and 41 RBIs across 66 games. Ben Rice shouldered much of the load, fulfilling Boone’s spring prediction of 39 homers.
Bellinger remains an impactful force, while Luis García Jr.’s increased bat speed suggests his production is sustainable despite a recent slump. Meanwhile, Heliot Ramos has shown power after a sluggish start and will be leaned upon in the playoffs against left-handed pitching.
“We know we’re capable of winning games,” said Boone, who noted the club’s 36-24 record since the All-Star break, most of which occurred without Judge. “We’ve had to play without a lot of key pieces at different points and for large chunks of this season.”
The kids are all right
George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones opened eyes during the club’s recent series against the Diamondbacks, when they crushed a Statcast-calculated combined 872 feet of home runs against Corbin Burnes – big-boy blasts of 424 and 448 feet, respectively, that suggested they’re growing more comfortable in The Show.
There have been growing pains across their first months of big league activity, with Lombard committing errors in six consecutive games over one span and Jones showing the swing-and-miss that will probably always be part of his game. But the talent is real, and no one should be surprised if either rookie delivers in a big October moment.
“We really just have to play for each other; lean on each other, pass the baton,” Bellinger said. “You do your job and control what you can.”
Improving health
While Judge’s outlook is cloudy, the Yankees are slowly becoming more whole.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. was activated from the injured list between games of Tuesday’s doubleheader, restoring a dynamic presence. It has been a disappointing year overall, but Chisholm was hot at the time of his injury (18-for-46, .391). The Yanks will look for him to pick up where he left off.
Meanwhile, Anthony Volpe made the most of an opportunity in Chisholm’s absence, which could have earned him a spot on a playoff roster – especially if they go with 11 pitchers and 15 position players in the first round. Trent Grisham is thought to be in play for the playoff roster.
“Hopefully more people are able to join and make us more formidable along the way,” Boone said.
A bolstered bullpen
The Yankees’ relievers have been among the league’s best all year, but there have been concerning signs of late. Brent Headrick ranks second in the Majors with 79 appearances and has seen inconsistent velocity, for example, suggesting he could benefit from a breather once the AL East is decided. David Bednar and Paul Blackburn, meanwhile, remain sharp.
Because the Yankees would have no reason to roster five starting pitchers in October, help is on the way. Will Warren is scheduled to make one more start and then transition to a relief role, giving the ’pen an intriguing multi-inning option. Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers are also in the mix.
“That’s the beauty of the postseason; guys fall into different roles and a lot of times can become heroic in roles you didn’t necessarily count on at the start of the season,” Boone said.

item.content:encoded:
Field Level Media

23 Sep 2026, 08:10 GMT+10

(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Drew Rasmussen allowed one hit in 6 2/3 outstanding innings and the visiting Tampa Bay Rays clinched the AL East with a 6-1 victory over the New York Yankees on Tuesday night in the nightcap of a day-night doubleheader.
The Rays (96-61) won for the 20th time in 28 games and clinched their fifth division title. Tampa Bay last won the AL East in 2021 when it won a team-record 100 games.
Tampa Bay also claimed division titles in the pandemic shortened 2020 season, 2010 and 2008 and will head to the postseason as the top seed in the AL.
Rasmussen (16-5) took a no-hitter into the seventh until Heliot Ramos opened the inning with a double to left. Ramos eventually scored on an RBI single by rookie George Lombard Jr. off Kevin Kelly.
Rasmussen finished with 11 strikeouts for his fourth career double-digit strikeout performance. He finished two shy of his career-high set June 10 against the Boston Red Sox and the Rays won his 12th consecutive start.
Rasmussen threw a career-high 114 pitches and struck out New York leadoff hitter Ben Rice twice. He also struck out rookie Spencer Jones to end the fourth after allowing a walk to Cody Bellinger, who he fanned in the first inning.
The right-hander exited after walking Jazz Chisholm Jr. and Kelly retired Austin Wells following Lombard's hit.
Yandy Diaz drove in two runs with a single in the seventh off reliever John Schreiber. Diaz added another two-run single in the ninth. The Rays scored their first run in the third when Ryan Vilade grounded out against New York's Max Fried (5-5), scoring Taylor Walls.
Cam Booser pitched a 1-2-3 eighth and Bryan Baker put two on in the ninth before retiring Lombard to secure the division crown.
Fried allowed four runs on six hits in 6 2/3 innings. The left-hander struck out four, walked two and notched 10 ground ball outs.
--Field Level Media

item.content:encoded:
Rays' Drew Rasmussen loses no-hit bid in 7th inning on leadoff double by Heliot Ramos
NEW YORK (AP) — Tampa Bay right-hander Drew Rasmussen lost a no-hit bid against the New York Yankees on Tuesday night when Heliot Ramos led off the seventh inning with a double.
The Rays, attempting to clinch the AL East title, had a 4-0 lead when Ramos lined a 1-2 sinker to left field, two pitches after hitting a foul ball down the right field line.
Before losing his no-hit bid, Rasmussen had 10 strikeouts and has thrown 93 pitches, 59 for strikes through six innings.
Matt Garza is the only Tampa Bay pitcher to throw a no-hitter. Garza no-hit Detroit on July 26, 2010, at Tropicana Field.
Rasmussen ended the sixth inning by getting New York's Cody Bellinger on a flyball to right field.
Rasmussen walked Austin Wells with one out in the third and ended the inning by striking out Ben Rice on a high fastball. The 31-year-old issued a leadoff walk to Cody Bellinger and ended the fourth by striking out rookie Spencer Jones with a fastball.
Rasmussen got consecutive strikeouts on rookie George Lombard Jr. and Austin Wells to finish the fifth at 78 pitches.
The Rays can claim their fifth AL East title with a victory and took a 1-0 lead on Ryan Vilade’s groundout in the third against Max Fried. They added three in the seventh on a bunt single by Taylor Walls and a two-run base hit by Yandy Diaz.
The Yankees have been no-hit eight times. The last was a combined no-hitter by Houston’s Cristian Javier, Hector Neris and Ryan Pressly on June 25, 2022, at Yankee Stadium.

item.title: [blogs.fangraphs.com] Yankees Face Judge Dread
item.dc:creator: Michael Baumann
item.description: When Aaron Judge is healthy, he’s the most dangerous hitter in baseball. item.content:encoded:
When Aaron Judge is healthy, he’s the most dangerous hitter in baseball. Sometimes I get alarmed at how uncontroversial a statement that is; ours is a sport that so frequently humiliates those who make such sweeping, unequivocal judgments as those.
But the empirical evidence is what it is. Judge has played 150 or more games in a season four times in his career. In those four seasons, he’s led all position players in WAR four times and led the league in wRC+ three times. He’s been named AL MVP three times and finished second once, ahead of some real doozies: Cal Raleigh’s 60-homer year, Bobby Witt Jr.’s 10.5-WAR campaign in 2024, Shohei Ohtani’s best pitching season — in fact, a healthy Judge is the only thing that’s ever trumped a healthy Ohtani in an MVP race.
So again, it’s not uncontroversial to say that when Judge is healthy he’s the best hitter in the world. He has not, however, always been healthy. Least of all this season, when he missed three months with a broken rib. And now, the single-season AL home run king is back on the IL with a calf strain. The timing could not be worse.
Judge last played on Wednesday, leaving open the option to activate him on Sunday for the final game of the regular season. That seems like a theoretical concern at the moment rather than a practical one. Our Matt Martell was at Yankee manager Aaron Boone’s pregame media availability on Tuesday morning, where Boone illustrated the inadequacy of a return-to-play timeline at this point in the season.
“We’re planning on [Judge] not being a part of [the Wild Card Series],” Boone said. “You hear all the time with injuries, we give ranges: two to four weeks, four to six. They’re ranges for a reason. We’re at a point in the year where, obviously, we’d push it a little bit if that was in play, but that’s a week away. I’m not expecting it, but I’m not ruling it out either.”
That’s the problem. A range of two weeks in recovery time isn’t a big deal in a six-month season, but even one week is twice as long as the Yankees’ entire first playoff round. And muscle injuries can be finicky to begin with — you go to bed one night feeling fine and wake up the next morning with weakness or stiffness.
For what it’s worth, the Yankees are technically still alive in the AL East race as of this writing, but you can forgive Boone for speaking as if the division is already lost.
Either way, in order to speed things along, Judge received a platelet-poor plasma (PPP) injection on Monday, not to be confused with a platelet-rich plasma (PRP) injection.
Now, apparently having read The Magic School Bus Inside the Human Body as a child is not a sufficient qualification to perform surgery on live patients. At least, that’s what the police told me. But anyone who’s read that book can tell you the makeup of human blood: Red blood cells, which carry oxygen; white blood cells, which fight infection; platelets, which stop bleeding and heal wounds; and plasma, which is the broth all the other stuff floats around in.
PRP injections are a pretty common treatment for sports injuries, but taking the healing bits out of plasma seems kind of counterintuitive. Sort of like a vodka-poor screwdriver. But evidently PPP contains high levels of fibrinogen, which is itself a healing agent. Ms. Frizzle didn’t cover fibrinogen, but sure, I’ll buy it.
Unless the PPP works an actual miracle, though, it looks like the Yankees are going to have to navigate at least the first round of the playoffs without their best player.
And even if Judge does return — either in the Wild Card round or later, if the Yankees advance — I’d caution against assuming that we’d be seeing the best of him right off the proverbial bat. For starters, 99% of star athletes in history are going to try to force their way into the lineup for the playoffs regardless of whether they’re actually healthy.
To say nothing of the fact that Judge can be streaky. This is the nature of Judge’s unusual skill set; there are 1,073 hitters in major league history with at least 5,000 career plate appearances. Judge is the only one of those who’s produced one of the three true outcomes (home run, strikeout, walk) in more than half of his career plate appearances. (I’d like to express my immense gratitude to Adam Dunn, who has a career TTO% of 49.9, for making this fun fact possible.)
Living on the extremes, as he does, Judge will have weeks where he homers every night, and others where he goes 1-for-20 with 12 strikeouts. But you live with it because, over a long enough timeline, it works out heavily in his favor. Among hitters with at least 5,000 career plate appearances, Judge has the third-highest career wRC+, trailing only Babe Ruth and Ted Williams. If you wanted to go further than “best hitter now” and anoint Judge the best hitter ever, leaning heavily on the argument that quality of competition increases over time, you’d have a credible case.
But that’s not what the Yankees got out of Judge this year. In 66 regular-season games, he’s hit .241/.360/.511, with his highest strikeout rate (29.8%) since 2019 and lowest wRC+ (141) since 2020. In seven games since he returned from his rib injury, Judge was just 4-for-23 with one home run, one walk, and 13 strikeouts.
I’ve done enough of these injury reaction posts to figure out that they’re not really about the guy who got hurt, but about the teammates he’s leaving behind.
And I don’t want to underrate the value of Judge — even the version of Judge that has a 141 wRC+, rather than a 200 wRC+ — but the Yankees have done OK without him.
In the weakest American League field in decades, the Yankees are one of only two teams with a winning percentage of .550 or better. Entering their doubleheader with the Rays on Tuesday, the Yankees are still first in the AL in home runs (216) and second in runs scored per game (4.60). Even without Judge (or Giancarlo Stanton, for that matter), their lineup has plenty of beef.

Ben Rice in particular has been absolutely terrific this season. He’s fourth among qualified AL hitters in wRC+ and third in both home runs and runs scored. The Astros have AL MVP frontrunner Yordan Alvarez in their lineup; apart from him, is there any hitter in the AL bracket who’s been Rice’s equal this year? Maybe Junior Caminero? Willson Contreras, if you value OBP over raw power? Even if you’re being charitable, it’s a short list.
Now, past Rice, things get interesting, because if you want to talk about the Yankees’ offensive depth, you have to be able to hold multiple ideas in your head at once.
As of Tuesday morning, the Yankees have 11 hitters with double-digit home runs this season, which is tied for the most in the league. That’s just counting players who have hit 10 or more home runs in pinstripes, and the Yankees brought in substantial reinforcements midseason. Luis García Jr. has just seven homers for the Yankees but 30 overall. Heliot Ramos has four home runs in 32 games and 13 overall, with 20-plus in each of his previous two seasons. George Lombard Jr. has just five home runs in 37 major league games, but he hit 12 dingers in 78 minor league games before he got called up.
Count all this up and the Yankees have more hitters with at least decent pop than they can fit on the roster at once.
At the same time, Rice is the only Yankee with 20 home runs in pinstripes this year. So while this lineup is short on automatic outs, if Judge is out, there’s a massive drop-off after Rice.
If you take Judge out of the picture, Cody Bellinger is second on the Yankees in wRC+, at 119. The Rays don’t have anyone with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Rice this season, but they have four hitters (Caminero, Yandy Díaz, Jonathan Aranda, and Victor Mesa Jr.) with 100 or more plate appearances and a better wRC+ than Bellinger. So do the Rangers (Justin Foscue, Josh Jung, Joc Pederson, Wyatt Langford). The Astros have Alvarez, plus Isaac Paredes and Jeremy Peña. The White Sox have Miguel Vargas, Munetaka Murakami, and Tristan Peters.
As good as Rice has been, the Yankees’ lineup looks concerningly pedestrian without Judge. If you aren’t already a FanGraphs Member, please consider becoming one; it’s the only way to get trenchant original analysis like this.
The good news is that Judge’s calf injury runs counter to the rest of the team’s injury luck. Carlos Rodón, who missed almost three months with an elbow injury earlier this year, dominated the Rays in eight scoreless innings in Game 1 of a doubleheader on Tuesday. The same day, the Yankees activated Chisholm, who’d spent two weeks on the IL with a sprained thumb. Clarke Schmidt just returned from Tommy John surgery last week, and while he suffered biceps cramping in the bullpen on Sunday, it appears to be a minor setback. Trent Grisham remains a question mark for the start of the playoffs as he recovers from a hamstring injury, but his prognosis also looks good.
Judge is as important to the Yankees as any two or three other players put together, but with a healthy and deep rotation and Rice leading the way offensively, they’re not in bad shape. The remainder of this roster could easily survive and advance through a weaker AL bracket, setting the stage for a dramatically timed Judge return in mid-October. Like Kirk Gibson, only bigger.
Michael is a writer at FanGraphs. Previously, he was a staff writer at The Ringer and D1Baseball, and his work has appeared at Grantland, Baseball Prospectus, The Atlantic, ESPN.com, and various ill-remembered Phillies blogs. Follow him on Twitter, if you must, @MichaelBaumann.

item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge is out, and the Yankees don’t know when — or if — he’ll be back.
So if they’re going to go anywhere in the playoffs, they’ll almost certainly have to do some work without him.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
That means Cody Bellinger’s role will be even more important than it’s been for much of the season, and lately, he’s answered the call.
It was Bellinger’s two-run shot in Game 1 on Tuesday that provided all the scoring in the 2-0 win over Tampa Bay in The Bronx.
The blast was Bellinger’s 17th of the season and fifth in his past 12 games.
With Judge out indefinitely with a strained right calf, Aaron Boone said the team was “not expecting” Judge to be available for the wild-card series that begins next week.
As Bellinger said following the win in Tuesday’s opener, any chance the Yankees have without Judge will be due to a collective effort.
But there’s little doubt that Bellinger — whose $36.5 million salary this year is second only to Judge’s $40 million — will be called upon more than most.
Against right-hander Nick Martinez of Tampa Bay, Bellinger hit second — a spot that he and Ben Rice have mostly split in Judge’s absence.
Rice doubled off Martinez to lead off the bottom of the fourth of a scoreless game, and Bellinger followed with his shot out to right.
“[Rice] had a great at-bat in front of me [and] saw a lot of pitches,’’ Bellinger said. “It was a close game. I’m not trying to do too much at all. I want to keep it really simple, put a good swing on the ball.”
It’s the approach the Yankees are hoping to have without Judge, whose “moderate” strain has put their October plans in jeopardy.
“I think for us, it’s one game at a time,’’ Bellinger said. “We all believe in each other in this locker room. We’re not looking too far ahead.”
But it’s hard not to wonder how the lineup — and team — will withstand another Judge absence.
“Having Judge on our team helps us tremendously,’’ Bellinger said. “We’ve just got to continue to come out and win games, playing for each other, leaning on each other [and] playing good baseball.”
As the Yankees have noted, they’ve stayed in the postseason picture, even as Judge missed three-plus months with a fractured rib this summer.
Shop Yankees Merch
“We have a lot of talent in this locker room, a lot of depth,” Bellinger said. “A lot of different guys stepped up, whether it’s their first year in the big leagues or getting traded [here]. We keep playing winning baseball.”
Bellinger added to that not just with his bat Tuesday, but with his arm, as well.
After Victor Mesa Jr. opened the sixth with a single off Carlos Rodón, Bellinger started an inning-ending double play two batters later when Richie Palacios lined out to left.
Mesa didn’t know where the ball was and didn’t get back to first in time to beat Bellinger’s strong throw.
“He went through that stretch when he was struggling and then got injured,’’ Boone said of Bellinger’s earlier slump and hamstring injury. “But he’s dialed in now and hitting line drives all over the ballpark. … It’s good to see as we get down the stretch.”

item.title: [New York Post] Yankees keep slim AL East hopes alive with shutout of Rays to open doubleheader
item.dc:creator: Mark W Sanchez
item.description:
A week or two ago, Tuesday’s doubleheader loomed as perhaps the largest day (and night) of the Yankees season. But the Rays separating themselves — entering with a six-game lead that had doubled since Sept. 11 — and requiring just one victory in this four-game set to clinch the division drained much of the drama from the opening game of the series at a half-filled Stadium.

item.content:encoded:
A week or two ago, Tuesday’s doubleheader loomed as perhaps the largest day (and night) of the Yankees season.
But the Rays separating themselves — entering with a six-game lead that had doubled since Sept. 11 — and requiring just one victory in this four-game set to clinch the division drained much of the drama from the opening game of the series at a half-filled Stadium.




Access the Yankees beat like never before


Join Post Sports+ for exciting subscriber-only features, including real-time texting with Greg Joyce about the inside buzz on the Yankees.
Try it free
And so a strong afternoon effort by the Yankees encouraged and kept their AL East hopes alive, but it more kept those hopes on a ventilator than revive them.
In the first of two games on the day, the Yankees beat the Rays 2-0 in front of an announced crowd of 41,421 in The Bronx during a brisk late-September afternoon that hinted at October.
In all likelihood, also coming soon is the Rays wrapping up the division, but the Yankees (90-66) at least did not allow their rival to celebrate on their grass immediately. Of course, the Rays (95-61) have three more chances to do so, including another that was set for just a few hours later.
“We all believe in each other in this locker room and not looking too far ahead,” said Cody Bellinger, who provided the only run-scoring swing in the victory that clinched no worse than the top wild-card spot.
The Yankees are nearly guaranteed a first-round home date with the Red Sox in a best-of-three series that likely would not include their best player: The club is operating under the belief Aaron Judge will not be available for the series because of his calf strain.
If Aaron Boone’s bunch is going to escape the Red Sox and face off with these same Rays in the ALDS, they would have to rely on their stars rather than their superstar.
On that front, Tuesday afternoon provided some hope with Carlos Rodón (eight shutout, overpowering innings in which he faced just one over the minimum) and Bellinger (a two-run blast in the fourth inning that provided the only runs the club needed) stepping up.
“Just a really solid, quick win,” Boone said of a game that lasted just 2 hours, 2 minutes in large part because of Rodón’s dominance and efficiency, which bodes well for the postseason even if Rodón probably would not get a first-round start.
In his longest, best and likely last outing of the regular season, Rodón struck out eight and allowed just three base runners on three singles.
The first two were erased by double plays (the second, in the sixth inning, entailed Bellinger catching a Richie Palacios line drive and throwing strong to first to double up Victor Mesa Jr.).
The third was a one-out single to Jonathan Aranda in the seventh inning, which might have presented the greatest threat to Rodón. But against Junior Caminero — an MVP candidate who represented the tying run — the veteran reached back for his two hardest pitches of the game (both 97.5 mph fastballs) to get ahead 0-2 before finishing Caminero off with a slider.
“He was awesome. Strike throwing was great,” Boone said of Rodón, who needed 96 pitches to record 24 outs, won his 100th career game and tallied his 1,500th strikeout. “… [He had] velo when he really needed it.”
The Yankees offense was held down by Nick Martinez for three perfect innings before pouncing on two consecutive imperfect pitches to begin the bottom of the fourth.
Ben Rice roped a double down the right field line for the first Yankees hit before Bellinger got a first-pitch sinker across the middle of the plate and clubbed it to right for his 17th homer of the season.
And that was all Rodón needed in a game that might have given the club a blueprint for how it can succeed in October against a team like the Rays and without a monstrous presence like Judge.
“You see the defense today — we’re solid,” said Rodón, who praised José Caballero (a bunt single and two steals in an empty fifth inning) before addressing the rest of the club. “Some lengthy at-bats. Some big-time hits — the homer from Beli there. The bullpen is deep.
“The starters are really good. I have a lot of confidence in this club.”

item.title: [cbsnews.com] Carlos Rodón dominant over 8 innings as Yankees top Rays in doubleheader opener
item.dc:creator: CBS New York Team
item.description: Carlos Rodón allowed three hits in eight sharp innings and the New York Yankees prevented the Tampa Bay Rays from clinching the AL East title with a 2-0 victory in the opener of a day-night doubleheader on Tuesday. The Yankees (90-66) moved six games ahead of the Red Sox for the AL's top wild-card spot. Tampa Bay (95-61) has a magic number of two to clinch the AL East for the fifth time in team history and first since 2021. Cody Bellinger hit a two-run homer in the fourth inning off Tampa Bay st
item.content:encoded:
Carlos Rodón allowed three hits in eight sharp innings and the New York Yankees prevented the Tampa Bay Rays from clinching the AL East title with a 2-0 victory in the opener of a day-night doubleheader on Tuesday.
The Yankees (90-66) moved six games ahead of the Red Sox for the AL's top wild-card spot. Tampa Bay (95-61) has a magic number of two to clinch the AL East for the fifth time in team history and first since 2021.
Cody Bellinger hit a two-run homer in the fourth inning off Tampa Bay starter Nick Martinez (15-5) and also started a key double play to end the sixth by throwing out Victor Mesa Jr. at first.
Rodón (7-3) struck out eight and walked none while completing eight innings for the first time since July 11, 2025, against the Cubs. The left-hander, who recorded his 100th win, became the 18th active pitcher to reach 1,500 career strikeouts when he fanned Jonny DeLuca on a slider for the second out of the eighth.
Rodón also struck out AL MVP candidate Junior Caminero on a slider in the dirt in the seventh with a runner on after reaching 98 mph on the previous two pitches.
Rodón threw first-pitch strikes to 15 of 25 hitters and improved to 3-1 in seven starts since returning from left elbow inflammation last month.
Following a double by Ben Rice off Martinez in the fourth, Bellinger lifted the next pitch into the right field seats for a 2-0 lead.
After a single by Mesa started the sixth, Richie Palacios lifted a fly ball to Bellinger. Bellinger made the catch and a strong one-hop throw to first baseman Luis García Jr. to easily complete the double play and get his eighth outfield assist this year.
Martinez allowed two runs and five hits in six innings. The right-hander struck out seven and lost for the first time since July 9.
David Bednar retired Yandy Díaz for his 35th save in 39 chances and finish New York's 15th shutout in 2 hours, 2 minutes - the Yankees' fastest game this season.
Up next
Tampa Bay RHP Drew Rasmussen (15-5, 2.72 ERA) opposes New York LHP Max Fried (5-4, 2.63) in the second game.

item.title: [pinstripealley.com] Yankees win first game of doubleheader behind Carlos Rodón’s milestone performance
item.dc:creator: Peter Brody
item.description: The chances are now paper thin after a series loss in Arizona, but if the Yankees are to have any shot of chasing down the Rays in the final week of the season, they absolutely must sweep this four-game series. That required a dominant performance from Carlos Rodón facing one of the AL’s best starters in Nick Martinez. They certainly got that, Rodón running rampant for eight scoreless innings, achieving both the 1,500th strikeout and 100th win of his career as the Yankees took the first game of
item.content:encoded:
The chances are now paper thin after a series loss in Arizona, but if the Yankees are to have any shot of chasing down the Rays in the final week of the season, they absolutely must sweep this four-game series. That required a dominant performance from Carlos Rodón facing one of the AL’s best starters in Nick Martinez. They certainly got that, Rodón running rampant for eight scoreless innings, achieving both the 1,500th strikeout and 100th win of his career as the Yankees took the first game of the day’s doubleheader, 2-0.
Rodón burst out of the gate like he had a point to prove, whiffing the first two batters of the game Yandy Díaz and Jonathan Aranda on a pair of filthy sliders. Cam Schlittler and Max Fried are likely locks for the postseason rotation, meaning if the Yankees elect to stick with a three-man unit, that final spot comes down to Rodón and Gerrit Cole. Aaron Boone has affirmed his commitment to Cole as the Game One starter in a prospective Wild Card Series. This seemingly leaves Rodón on the bubble, which might explain the extra edge he was pitching with this afternoon.
His teammates didn’t do themselves any favors early, burning both ABS challenges in the first inning. I expect the Yankees to tighten the strings on who gets to challenge and in what situation come the playoffs as you cannot deprive yourself of such a vital tool with eight innings still to play.
Martinez entered this game with the lowest walk rate of any qualified starter and among the league’s best at limiting hard contact. He was true to form going the first turn through the order without allowing a base runner. He was helped by the collectively poor approach from the lineup, with four out of the nine batters including the side in the third striking out against a pitcher with the lowest strikeout rate among qualified starters.
That started to change the second turn through the order, the Yankees finally starting to do some damage against the high volume of pitches Martinez was throwing over the heart of the plate, starting with a Ben Rice double into the corner in right to lead off the fourth. The very next pitch Martinez threw rocketed out of the yard, Cody Bellinger blasting a first pitch sinker into the seats in right for a two-run homer — his fifth homer in the last 12 games.
George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones singled with two outs to put runners on the corners. Jones then stole second unopposed, but Anthony Volpe struck out swinging to strand the pair in scoring position. They kept up the pressure in the fifth, José Caballero reaching on a bunt single against his former team and then stealing second and third followed by a Rice walk to put runners on the corners with one out. However, Bellinger popped out and Heliot Ramos flew out as they stranded a pair in consecutive frames.
Rodón settled into an impressive groove after a Chandler Simpson single in the second, retiring the next ten batters in order until Victor Mesa Jr. led off the sixth with a single. After Rodón whiffed Jorge Mateo on a slider for his sixth strikeout, he got Richie Palacios to line out to left. Mesa was running on the play and momentarily forget he had to sprint back to first, allowing Bellinger to throw an absolute seed to Luis García Jr., who applid the tag for the inning-ending double play.
With Rodón’s pitch count standing at just 89 after seven, Boone decided to go batter-to-batter in the eighth. However, Rodón ensured his manager had no choice to make, completing the eighth inning on just seven pitches, including the 1,500th strikeout of his career. It’s tied for his longest start as a Yankee, matching the eight innings he pitched against the Cubs on July 11, 2025.
Rodón entered this start as perhaps the Yankees’ most in-form pitcher behind Schlittler. Including today, in his last eight starts, Rodón has a 1.67 ERA while holding batters to a measly .134 batting average against. He had all his pitches working today, but this really felt like a throwback to his peak years with Chicago and San Francisco. He got whiffs in bunches on the four-seamer above the zone and slider below it. In likely his penultimate start of the regular season, Rodón dominated for eight scoreless innings, allowing three hits and no walks while striking out eight to lower his ERA to 2.67 on the year.
The Yankees didn’t manage another base runner in the final three innings, but Rodón made sure that it wouldn’t come back to haunt them. David Bednar pitched a one-two-three ninth to secure his 35th save of the season. The gap to the Rays now stands at five games as the Yankees become the second team in the AL to 90 wins. At worst, they have clinched the four seed in the AL, guaranteeing home field advantage in a prospective AL Wild Card Series.
The Yankees have a few hours’ rest before taking the field again tonight. Max Fried starts the night game of the doubleheader against Drew Rasmussen. First pitch is scheduled for 7:05 pm ET with the broadcast remaining on YES, so stick around!

item.title: [fingerlakes1.com] Carlos Rodón dominates as Yankees shut out Rays in Game 1 of doubleheader | Fingerlakes1.com
item.dc:creator: Facebook Com; Fingerlakes1; Kyle Evans
item.description: Carlos Rodón delivered his best starts of the season Tuesday afternoon, leading the New York Yankees to a 2-0 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in the first game of a doubleheader at Yankee Stadium. Rodón allowed only three hits, all singles, while striking out eight over eight scoreless innings. It was his first eight-inning performance since July 11, 2025. The left-hander retired 19 straight batters at one point, with two double plays helping preserve the perfect stretch. Jose Caballero started
item.content:encoded:
Carlos Rodón delivered his best starts of the season Tuesday afternoon, leading the New York Yankees to a 2-0 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in the first game of a doubleheader at Yankee Stadium.
Rodón allowed only three hits, all singles, while striking out eight over eight scoreless innings. It was his first eight-inning performance since July 11, 2025.
The left-hander retired 19 straight batters at one point, with two double plays helping preserve the perfect stretch. Jose Caballero started a 5-4-3 double play in the second inning, while Cody Bellinger caught a line drive in the third before throwing to first base, where Luis García Jr. tagged Victor Mesa Jr. trying to return to the bag.
Rodón also reached a career milestone in the eighth inning when he recorded his 1,500th strikeout. His season earned-run average dropped to 2.67, while he has posted a 1.42 earned-run average in four September starts.
New York’s offense struggled to generate much against Tampa Bay starter Nick Martinez, who retired the Yankees in order the first time through the lineup.
That changed in the fourth inning. Ben Rice opened the frame with a double before Bellinger followed with a two-run home run to right field, giving New York its only runs of the game.
George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones followed with consecutive two-out singles, but Anthony Volpe struck out to end the inning.
David Bednar closed the game with a scoreless ninth for his 35th save.
The victory moved New York to within five games of Tampa Bay in the American League East.
The teams meet again Tuesday at 7:05 p.m. Max Fried starts for New York against Drew Rasmussen.

item.content:encoded:
Yankees hold off Rays' celebration with win in doubleheader opener
(Photo credit: Brad Penner)
Cody Bellinger hit a two-run home run in the fourth inning as the host New York Yankees recorded a 2-0 victory over the Tampa Bay Rays in the opener of a day-night doubleheader on Tuesday.
With the victory, the Yankees (90-66) prevented the Rays (95-61) from clinching the AL East and moved six games ahead of the Boston Red Sox for the American League's top wild-card spot.
Tampa Bay still has a magic number of two to clinch the fifth divisional title in team history and first since 2021.
New York's Carlos Rodon (7-3) scattered three singles over eight innings as the Yankees finished off the victory in a brisk 2 hours, 2 minutes. Rays right-hander Nick Martinez (15-5) allowed two runs on five hits over six innings with seven strikeouts to take his first loss since July 9.
Rodon allowed singles to Chandler Simpson in the second, Victor Mesa Jr. in the sixth and Jonathan Aranda in the seventh. The left-hander struck out eight in his 100th career win and longest outing since he went eight innings against the Chicago Cubs on July 11, 2025.
Rodon also reached 1,500 strikeouts when he set down Jonny DeLuca on a slider in the eighth.
Martinez retired the first nine Yankees hitters of the game before Ben Rice laced a double to right field to lead off the fourth inning and Bellinger hammered the next pitch to the right-field seats for a 2-0 lead.
It was Bellinger's 17th home run and sixth in his past 26 games.
Bellinger also started a key double play from left field to end the sixth. After Mesa opened the inning with a single, Richie Palacios lofted a fly ball to left with Bellinger making the catch then firing a one-hop throw to first baseman Luis Garcia Jr. to complete the double play.
It was Bellinger's eighth outfield assist of the season.
David Bednar finished New York's 15th shutout by retiring Yandy Diaz for his 35th save.
--Field Level Media

item.title: [fansided.com] Projecting the Yankees Wild Card series lineup after brutal Aaron Judge's injury update
item.dc:creator: Zachary Rotman
item.description: It felt like Aaron Judge was returning at the perfect time. A September return following a three-month stint on the IL gave Judge enough time to find his timing before the postseason. Unfortunately, Judge suffered another injury before the playoffs even began, hurting his calf in a game against the Minnesota Twins. The New York Yankees hoped it'd be minor, but it was serious enough for the team to place its captain on the Injured List. Now, it sounds as if a return for the Yankees' first postsea
item.content:encoded:
It felt like Aaron Judge was returning at the perfect time. A September return following a three-month stint on the IL gave Judge enough time to find his timing before the postseason. Unfortunately, Judge suffered another injury before the playoffs even began, hurting his calf in a game against the Minnesota Twins. The New York Yankees hoped it'd be minor, but it was serious enough for the team to place its captain on the Injured List. Now, it sounds as if a return for the Yankees' first postseason series is a long shot at best.
A "moderate grade" calf strain is serious enough for Yankees manager Aaron Boone to proceed as if his best player won't be active at all for the Wild Card series. That is an insanely difficult blow for a Yankees team that, with Judge, is as good as any in a weak American League. For the Yankees to advance to the ALDS and potentially get their captain back, they'll need to rely on this projected lineup below.
What the Yankees lineup could look like without Aaron Judge
Judge is an instrumental piece in the Yankees' lineup for a couple of reasons. First, he's the best hitter in the sport when healthy. That obviously matters. Second, Judge is one of the few right-handed bats on this roster. He provides much-needed balance that, without Judge, the Yankees lack.
| Position | Player |
|---|---|
| Ben Rice | DH |
| Cody Bellinger | LF |
| Heliot Ramos | RF |
| Luis Garcia Jr. | 1B |
| Spencer Jones | CF |
| George Lombard Jr. | SS |
| Jazz Chisholm Jr. | 2B |
| Austin Wells | C |
| Jose Caballero | 3B |
This lineup still has some good pieces in it. Ben Rice has had a breakout year, Cody Bellinger is a well-rounded star, and trails only Yordan Alvarez and Pete Crow-Armstrong, the AL and NL MVP favorites, with a .532 slugging percentage. If Jazz Chisholm Jr. can return from the IL looking like the player he's capable of being, the Yankees can score runs.
The problem, though, is that six of the nine hitters in this lineup are left-handed, and most of them are much better against righties than lefties. The Yankees will use guys like Paul Goldschmidt and Amed Rosario against left-handed pitching, but having Heliot Ramos, who has a .672 OPS since being acquired by the Yankees at the deadline, in the No. 3 hole against righties isn't ideal. The Yankees don't have much of a choice with Judge out, though.
Ultimately, with Judge out, this is a team heavily reliant on lineup platoons. It'll be on Aaron Boone to try to push the right buttons in order to get this offense, which has been remarkably inconsistent without Judge, to score runs against (likely) a potent Boston Red Sox pitching staff.
Aaron Judge injury update: Can the Yankees expect their star to return?
What's most frustrating about the Judge injury update is that we have no idea what the injury is. The Yankees, for whatever reason, keep information regarding injuries, particularly to Judge, extremely close to the vest, making it difficult to know when or even if Judge will be back. All we know is that Judge is dealing with what Aaron Boone deems a "moderate" strain.
That doesn't sound good, especially for a player who has had trouble with the same right calf in the past. In the shortened 2020 season, Judge attempted to return from a calf strain in a couple of weeks, but wound up re-aggravating the injury, pushing his return back several weeks. Calf injuries and other soft-tissue ailments are not to be messed with, and can lead to a major setback if rushed through.
Plus, if the injury was minor, wouldn't the Yankees be quick to tell the world that? I'd love to say Judge is a lock to return at some point, but even if the Yankees were to advance to the ALDS, given how little we know and how tricky returns can be from calf injuries, it's probably wishful thinking to assume he'd be back right at the start of a potential ALDS, which is the last thign any New York fan wants to hear.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees Announce Paul Goldschmidt Decision Before Rays Doubleheader
item.dc:creator: Jonathan Vankin
item.description: The New York Yankees are coming off two straight losses in Arizona to the Diamondbacks, a setback that left them a full six games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East pennant race. item.content:encoded:
The New York Yankees are coming off two straight losses in Arizona to the Diamondbacks, a setback that left them a full six games behind the Tampa Bay Rays in the American League East pennant race.
But the Yankees still have a chance to win the division and with it, the top seed in the AL and a bye out of the Wild card playoff round.
The Yankees and Rays open a four-game, head-to-head series with the first game of a doubleheader Tuesday at Yankee Stadium. With a four-game sweep, the Yankees would take the season tiebreaker and need to win at least two of three against the Baltimore Orioles, while the Rays lose two of three to the Philadelphia Phillies to close out the regular season.
Before Game One of the twin bill, the Yankees announced a decision on how they will utilize veteran first basinal Paul Goldschmidt.
Goldschmidt is out of the New York Yankees lineup for a third straight game, sidelined again by a stark platoon split against right-handed pitching.
The pattern has held all September, and it likely has fans wondering about how much longer the 39-year-old holds even a part-time role with October two weeks away.
| NEW YORK YANKEES STARTING LINEUP (GAME 1) | | | | |
| SP: Carlos Rodón (LHP) • 6-3, 2.95 ERA | | | | |
| September 22, 2026 • Yankee Stadium, Bronx, NY • 1:05 PM ET • Rays at Yankees | | | | |
| # | Player | Pos | AVG | SLG |
| 1 | Ben Rice | DH | .261 | .528 |
| 2 | Cody Bellinger | LF | .270 | .435 |
| 3 | Heliot Ramos | RF | .241 | .409 |
| 4 | Luis García Jr. | 1B | .281 | .532 |
| 5 | George Lombard Jr. | SS | .235 | .386 |
| 6 | Spencer Jones | CF | .248 | .442 |
| 7 | Anthony Volpe | 2B | .248 | .340 |
| 8 | Alí Sánchez | C | .250 | .316 |
| 9 | José Caballero | 3B | .236 | .373 |
| Lineups confirmed. Season stats shown (AVG / SLG). Umpire: Sean Barber • Weather: 63°, Wind 13 mph • O/U: 7 Runs • Line: TB +112 / NYY -135. | | | | |
Boone's Platoon Explains Goldschmidt Sit
Aaron Boone's lineup card for Tuesday's series opener against Tampa Bay leaves Goldschmidt out again, extending a run that traces back to Saturday. He started Friday against left-hander Eduardo Rodriguez in Arizona and went 1-for-4 with a walk and two runs, then sat both weekend games against right-handers Brandon Pfaadt and Corbin Burnes. That's three benchings in the last three games against right-handed starters.
Why? Goldschmidt has produced an elite 1.006 OPS against lefties this season but an anemic a .572 mark versus right-handers, a gap wide enough that Boone starts Ben Rice at DH and Luis García Jr. at first whenever a right-hander pitches. An Athletic report on the lineup moves after Aaron Judge's calf strain named Goldschmidt and Heliot Ramos as the bats Boone leans on against lefties, with García handling the right-handed side.
Nick Martinez, Tuesday's Tampa Bay starter, has largely dominated Goldschmidt in his career. The former National League MVP is 2-for-10 with four walks and two strikeouts against Martinez, and he is 0-for-13 with four strikeouts in his last three meetings with the right-hander since 2024. Martinez enters at 15-4 with a 2.94 ERA this year, and beat the Yankees in the Bronx in May, giving Boone both the season splits and the head-to-head history pointing toward a Goldschmidt benching.
Tuesday's day-night doubleheader against two more right-handed Rays starters gives Boone an easy excuse to sit the 39-year-old.
| TAMPA BAY RAYS STARTING LINEUP (GAME 1) | | | | |
| SP: Nick Martinez (RHP) • 15-4, 2.94 ERA | | | | |
| September 22, 2026 • Yankee Stadium, Bronx, NY • 1:05 PM ET • Rays at Yankees | | | | |
| # | Player | Pos | AVG | SLG |
| 1 | Yandy Díaz | DH | .292 | .449 |
| 2 | Jonathan Aranda | 1B | .277 | .440 |
| 3 | Junior Caminero | 3B | .277 | .529 |
| 4 | Liam Hicks | C | .288 | .440 |
| 5 | Chandler Simpson | LF | .309 | .360 |
| 6 | Jonny DeLuca | CF | .259 | .410 |
| 7 | Victor Mesa Jr. | RF | .251 | .502 |
| 8 | Ben Williamson | SS | .244 | .328 |
| 9 | Richie Palacios | 2B | .234 | .377 |
| Lineups confirmed. Season stats shown (AVG / SLG). Umpire: Sean Barber • Weather: 63°, Wind 13 mph • O/U: 7 Runs • Line: TB +112 / NYY -135. | | | | |
Goldschmidt's Future in New York
Goldschmidt turns free agent again this winter, and the Yankees have made no public commitment either way. A cheap return as a lefty-masher and clubhouse mentor remains plausible given Rice's grip on first base, and his credentials, a 2022 NL MVP award, seven All-Star selections, four Gold Gloves and five Silver Sluggers still makes him a name teams will inquire about this winter.
First base belongs to Rice, who has grown into an everyday role with 39 home runs and 95 RBI this season, pushing Goldschmidt into a complementary, short-side platoon job. That role fits the final stretch of a one-year, $4 million contract that can grow by $500,000 at each of four plate-appearance thresholds, according to Spotrac, a modest deal compared with the $12.5 million he earned in his first Yankees season a year earlier.

item.title: [MLB.com] Rays y Yankees se preparan para su serie crucial en el Bronx
item.dc:creator: Bryan Hoch; Adam Berry
item.description: NUEVA YORK -- Ha parecido inevitable que la lucha por el Este de la Liga Americana se decidiera esta semana en el Bronx. item.content:encoded:
NUEVA YORK -- Ha parecido inevitable que la lucha por el Este de la Liga Americana se decidiera esta semana en el Bronx.
Los Rays han encabezado la división más competitiva de Grandes Ligas durante gran parte de la temporada y no han cedido el primer lugar de la tabla desde que recuperaron la cima el 27 de junio.
Pero los Yankees siempre han estado ahí, amenazando y luego retrocediendo. Pero nunca han estado lo suficientemente lejos como para restarle importancia a lo que podría suceder esta semana.
Pues bien, llegó el momento.
Los Yankees recibirán a los Rays para una serie de cuatro juegos en el Yankee Stadium, comenzando con una doble-cartelera el martes. Gracias a la magnífica estadía de los Rays en casa y a la serie perdida por los Yankees en Phoenix frente a los Diamondbacks, la pregunta ahora es cuánto tiempo más seguirá viva esta lucha.
Los Rays llegaron a Nueva York con 6.0 juegos de ventaja en la división y apenas siete encuentros por disputarse. Una victoria de Tampa Bay eliminará a los Yankees de la lucha por la División Este y los dejará asegurados en un puesto del Comodín de la Liga Americana. Entonces, para que los Yankees tengan alguna posibilidad, deberán completar una barrida de cuatro partidos en tres días.
¿Lo que está en juego? Como dijo una vez Gerrit Cole: “Es mucho”. Entremos en materia.
¿Qué está en juego?
Rays: Ganar apenas un juego les garantizará a los Rays su primer campeonato del Este de la Liga Americana desde el 2021, otorgándoles un pase directo a la Serie Divisional y la ventaja de localía tanto en esa ronda como, si avanzan, en la Serie de Campeonato de la Liga Americana. También necesitan una sola victoria para asegurar la serie particular contra los Yankees.
Yankees: El piloto Aaron Boone reconoce que será una “tarea muy difícil” evitar que los Rays celebren con champaña en el Bronx, pero eso es exactamente lo que pretenden hacer. Empezaron la temporada buscando cambiar la narrativa, después de quedarse cortos ante los Azulejos el año pasado. En cambio, están a punto de tener que conformarse nuevamente con un premio de consolación y verse obligados a ganar una serie al mejor de tres juegos.
¿Cómo están alineadas las rotaciones?
Rays: Enviarán a sus mejores dos abridores al montículo para la doble-cartelera del martes. Primero será el derecho veterano Nick Martínez, líder del clubhouse y su fuente más confiable de innings. Tampa Bay tiene marca de 22-7 esta temporada en los juegos iniciados por el cubano-estadounidense. Después, le tocará a Drew Rasmussen, uno de los mejores abridores de la Liga Americana. Los Rays no han perdido una apertura de Rasmussen desde el 9 de julio, con marca perfecta de 11-0 en sus presentaciones desde entonces. Martínez lanzará con un día adicional de descanso, mientras que Rasmussen trabajará con cuatro días de descanso apenas por séptima vez esta campaña. El zurdo Ian Seymour y el derecho dominicano Freddy Peralta estarían alineados para abrir el miércoles y el jueves, respectivamente.
Yankees: Carlos Rodón y Max Fried abrirán los juegos de la doble-cartelera, en ese orden. Ambos han lidiado con lesiones esta temporada, pero están recuperando su mejor nivel en el momento indicado. En tres aperturas de septiembre, Rodón tiene marca de 2-0 con efectividad de 2.08, dejando atrás un episodio de inflamación en el codo izquierdo. Después de ingresar dos veces a la lista de lesionados por una contusión ósea en el codo de lanzar, Fried tiene récord de 1-0 y promedio de carreras limpias de 1.69 en tres aperturas este mes. Cole y Cam Schlittler, favorito para ganar el Premio Cy Young de la Liga Americana, seguirán en el tercer y cuarto partidos de la serie, respectivamente.
¿Qué ha estado funcionando bien últimamente para cada equipo?
Rays: ¿Todo? Los Rays acaban de registrar récord de 8-1 durante su última estadía en casa de la campaña regular y han ganado cuatro series consecutivas contra los Bravos, Astros, Atléticos y Medias Rojas. Desde que fueron barridos en una serie de cuatro partidos en el Fenway Park tras la pausa del Juego de Estrellas, tienen marca de 39-18, la mejor de la Gran Carpa desde el 20 de julio. Su pitcheo abridor se ha visto particularmente sólido, con efectividad de 2.81 este mes, sólo detrás de la de los Yankees. Como de costumbre, han encontrado distintas maneras de anotar carreras, incluyendo ataques tempraneros como el del domingo y un par de jonrones para dejar en el terreno al rival por parte del candidato al JMV de la Liga Americana, el dominicano Junior Caminero.
Yankees: De repente, estos Yankees se encuentran apoyándose en la fortaleza de su pitcheo, confiando en que la ofensiva terminará respondiendo. Ben Rice conectó su 39no cuadrangular, la mayor cantidad del equipo, cumpliendo una predicción que Boone hizo durante los Entrenamientos de Primavera. Rice dijo que Boone estaba bromeando con él, quedándose con “uno o dos” por debajo de la cifra que él prefería, así que habrá que estar atentos a Rice mientras busca su 40mo vuelacercas esta semana. Austin Wells ha conectado tres bambinazos en sus últimos seis encuentros, mientras que el puertorriqueño Heliot Ramos ha volado la cerca en sus últimos dos partidos. Podría ser una pieza importante si los Yankees quieren hacerse sentir en octubre.
¿Cuáles son algunas áreas de preocupación que podrían convertirse en un problema esta semana o en la postemporada?
Rays: Muchos jugadores de los Rays han dado un paso al frente, pero el primer bate del equipo, el cubano Yandy Díaz, ha tenido un mes complicado, con línea ofensiva de .229/.286/.357 en septiembre. Él marca la pauta para la alineación, así que obviamente será importante que llegue en su mejor nivel a octubre. Y esto es realmente buscarle la quinta pata al gato, considerando que tiene marca de 3-0 con un salvamento y efectividad de 1.42 este mes, pero Bryan Baker, líder de Grandes Ligas en salvamentos, suma más bases por bolas (cuatro) que ponches (dos) en siete presentaciones durante septiembre. También necesitarán que sea dominante en la postemporada.
Yankees: Más allá del tirón en la pantorrilla derecha de Aaron Judge, un asunto que los Yankees están manejando como si fuera un secreto del estado, comienzan a surgir preocupaciones sobre el estado del bullpen. La velocidad de Brent Headrick ha disminuido y el relevista podría estar mostrando señales de fatiga después de liderar las Mayores con 79 presentaciones. Tim Hill no ha sido la máquina automática de provocar rodados de años anteriores. Michael Fulmer permitió un jonrón que decidió un juego en Arizona. Pero no hay un asunto más importante que demostrar que pueden ganar sin Judge, el motor alrededor del cual gira su ofensiva. Tienen marca de 48-41 sin él, comparada con 41-25 cuando ha estado en acción.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] Aaron Judge Injury: Yankees Impact in Shifting AL Playoff Race
item.dc:creator: Patrick McAvoy; Unknown
item.description: Over the last few days, Aaron Judge has been the talk of Major League Baseball. Judge is back on the Injured List after returning from the IL for a brief seven-game stint. Judge has played in just 66 games this season and the biggest question in baseball is whether he will be able to return during the postseason. item.content:encoded:
Over the last few days, Aaron Judge has been the talk of Major League Baseball.
Judge is back on the Injured List after returning from the IL for a brief seven-game stint. Judge has played in just 66 games this season and the biggest question in baseball is whether he will be able to return during the postseason. If Judge is Judge, then the Yankees are built to make a run to the World Series. If Judge doesn't return, all of a sudden the Yankees look like a team that could have a short playoff run. On Monday, Joel Sherman of the New York Post gave an update that will could certainly impact the race.
"There's some strong possibility he doesn't play anymore," Sherman said. "Calf strains are notorious for when they heal, let them heal more because it is a re-injury area of the body."
At this point, the vibes aren't high or pointing towards a return for Judge. Calf injuries are tough. Jim Bowden of The Athletic reported that Judge is dealing with a soleus strain. The playoffs begin in eight days. On Sep. 29, the Yankees will begin a three-game Wild Card series, very likely against the Boston Red Sox.
If Sherman is correct and Judge doesn't return, it completely changes the calculus of the American League playoffs. A healthy Judge balances New York's lineup. Without him, the Yankees are lefty-heavy. Outside of Ben Rice, no other member of the Yankees has hit more than 20 homers as a member of New York this season. Luis García Jr. has 30 total homers, but has hit just seven in a Yankees uniform. The power threat isn't the same without Judge.
The Tide Is Shifting In the American League
New York will have to face off against the Red Sox in a three-game Wild Card series, barring something shocking happening. Even if the Yankees were to win, they would then have to go against the American League-leading Tampa Bay Rays in the American League Division Series. A brutal one-two punch, to say the least.
Without Judge, that arguably should make the Red Sox the favorites in a three-game set. New York's lineup is lefty-heavy. The Red Sox happen to be loaded from a left-handed pitching standpoint. The Red Sox could roll with Payton Tolle and Ranger Suárez in two out of three games. Plus, Garrett Crochet is close to returning in a bullpen role. Imagine a scenario in which the Red Sox start either Tolle or Suárez in a game and then get multiple innings out of a healthy Crochet afterward? That's the worst-case scenario for a Yankees lineup that is full of lefties.
If Boston advances, it would be a toss-up between the Red Sox and the Rays in an ALDS series. Then, either would be the favorite in the American League Championship Series over the Chicago White Sox, Cleveland Guardians or the Texas Rangers. Arguably, the Red Sox should be the favorites in the American League in general right now with Judge out, although it would be close. The Red Sox have been the best team in baseball since the end of June and now the path is a little clearer.
The American League runs through the American League East. If Judge was fully healthy, New York would be the favorites. The Yankees' rotation is electric and this team can seriously put up runs when Judge is at his best. Judge is the most impactful right-handed hitter in baseball. This is a guy who three out of the last four AL MVP awards, including the last two years in a row. When he's on the field, he moves the needle. Without him, the Yankees are still good, but they're not as big a World Series threat.
Patrick McAvoy's experiences include local and national sports coverage at the New England Sports Network with a focus on baseball and basketball. Outside of journalism, Patrick also received an MBA at Brandeis University. For all business/marketing inquiries regarding Fastball On SI, please reach out to Scott Neville: scott@moreviewsmedia.com

item.content:encoded:
We’ve made it to the final week of the regular season. There are still two divisions in the American League up for grabs, a couple of long-shot playoff hopefuls looking to make a last-minute run, and playoff seeding to fight over. It should make for a dramatic end to a great season.
Our power rankings use a modified Elo rating system. If you’re familiar with chess rankings, you’ll know that Elo is an elegant ranking format that measures teams’ relative strength and is very reactive to recent performance. To avoid overweighting recent results during the season, we weigh each team’s raw Elo rank using our coin flip playoff odds (specifically, we regress the playoff odds by 50% and weigh those against the raw Elo ranking, increasing in weight as the season progresses to a maximum of 25%). The weighted Elo ranks are then displayed as “Power Score” in the tables below. As the best and worst teams sort themselves out between now and October, they’ll filter to the top and bottom of the rankings, while the exercise remains reactive to hot streaks and cold snaps. If you’re looking for a visual representation of the ups and downs of your team throughout the season, look no further than the brand new Power Rankings Board in the FanGraphs Lab.
First up are the full rankings, presented in a sortable table. Below that, I’ve grouped the teams into tiers with comments on a handful of clubs. You’ll notice that the official ordinal rankings don’t always match the tiers — there are times where I take editorial liberties when grouping teams together — but generally, the ordering is consistent. One thing to note: The playoff odds listed in the tables below are our standard Depth Charts odds, not the coin flip odds that are used in the ranking formula.

It was a great week for the Brewers. They won their fourth straight NL Central title and sixth in the last nine years, and also set another franchise record for wins in a single season, one year after setting the previous record. They now have a chance to win 100 games for the first time in club history this week and still have the top seed in the NL to play for.
The Rays swept the Athletics and won their series against the Red Sox last week to put some distance between themselves and the Yankees in the AL East race. The gap in the division is now six games, and even though the two rivals play each other four times during the final week of the season, it would take a massive collapse from Tampa Bay to upset the current standings. Because the Rays also currently lead the season series with the Yankees, 6-3, all they need is to win one of the four games in New York to take the division title. With Shane McClanahan still recovering from his forearm injury — his availability for the playoffs is up in the air — Freddy Peralta has stepped up to lead the pitching staff over the last few weeks. Across his last five starts, he’s allowed just three runs in 28 2/3 innings. That’s the kind of production the Rays were hoping to get when they acquired him at the trade deadline.
| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Dodgers | 96-60 | 1580 | 1492 | 100.0% | 1621 |
| Padres | 87-69 | 1578 | 1501 | 97.2% | 1618 |
| Braves | 92-64 | 1565 | 1500 | 100.0% | 1610 |
| Yankees | 89-66 | 1556 | 1497 | 100.0% | 1603 |
The Dodgers are getting all their pieces in place for the postseason. Andy Pages and Roki Sasaki will be activated off the IL on Tuesday, and Shohei Ohtani should follow on Wednesday. There’s a lingering question about Blake Snell’s status after he injured his groin last week, but it sounds like he’ll be able to make a start during the final weekend of the season. And even though the majority of the year has been a slog for Kyle Tucker, his bat seems to have finally woken up at the right time; he collected nine hits and three home runs last week.
Having won 13 of their last 14 games, the Padres are peaking at exactly the right moment. They’ve surged five games ahead of the Diamondbacks and one ahead of the Phillies in the NL Wild Card standings, and are now tied with the Cubs for the top spot. San Diego’s final series of the season against Arizona still looms large, especially if the Friars stumble against the Dodgers in the series beforehand. You’re probably familiar with Fernando Tatis Jr.’s hot streak — he blasted four home runs last week to bring his total in September up to eight — but the biggest contributor to the Padres’ success recently has been Ty France. He had 12 hits and a home run last week and has posted a fantastic 168 wRC+ during the second half of the season.
After a couple of years away from the top, the Braves are NL East champions again — it’s their seventh division title in the last nine years. Atlanta’s dominance this year has been a welcome return to form. Even though his season has been a bit up and down, Ronald Acuña Jr. is looking like the superstar that won the MVP back in 2023 again. Last week, he smacked three home runs, including a go-ahead grand slam on Saturday, and is running a 191 wRC+ in September.
A little more than a week after being activated off the IL, Aaron Judge is back on the shelf, this time with a calf injury sustained on Wednesday. His availability for the playoffs is still up in the air, though he’s confident that he’ll be able to return sooner rather than later. Thankfully, Jazz Chisholm Jr. should be activated off the IL on Tuesday, and there’s some confidence that Trent Grisham will also be ready to return for the postseason. It helps that Ben Rice has bounced back from a rough August to post a 192 wRC+ in September. Still, Judge’s injury is a major blow to the Yankees’ hopes for a deep October run.
| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Red Sox | 84-72 | 1544 | 1500 | 100.0% | 1594 |
| Phillies | 86-70 | 1546 | 1501 | 97.3% | 1593 |
| Cubs | 87-69 | 1539 | 1501 | 99.9% | 1590 |
Even though the Red Sox lost both of their series last week, they managed to clinch a postseason berth on Sunday. It’s the cap to a remarkable turnaround after the team looked completely lost in mid-June. Boston can officially secure the second Wild Card spot with a couple of wins against the Guardians this week. Then the team can turn its attention to the Yankees and the rematch of last year’s Wild Card matchup between these two historic rivals.
Nothing is going to come easy for the Phillies over the next few weeks. The team placed Jesús Luzardo on the IL last week with a shoulder injury, but thankfully, it sounds like he’ll be ready to pitch in the playoffs. But before they count their chickens, they need to actually clinch a playoff spot. Philadelphia is four games up on the Diamondbacks in the NL Wild Card race, but its upcoming opponents are no cake walk; the Phillies have the Brewers and Rays on the schedule to finish off the regular season. Facing two of the best teams in baseball is quite a test ahead of the postseason, and the Phillies haven’t exactly been playing well lately.
The biggest concern for the Cubs right now is the status of Alex Bregman. He was struck by a foul ball in the face while standing in the on-deck circle during Sunday’s game and was taken to the hospital for further evaluation. Alongside Pete Crow-Armstrong, Bregman has been one of the best hitters in baseball since the All-Star break. It would be a huge blow if the third baseman had to miss any significant amount of time at this point in the season. As for Crow-Armstrong, he’s two stolen bases away from joining the 40/40 club. He put a few finishing touches on his MVP case last week by bopping four more home runs, bringing his season total up to 45.
| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Guardians | 81-75 | 1520 | 1498 | 97.6% | 1572 |
| White Sox | 80-76 | 1494 | 1500 | 96.2% | 1552 |
| Rangers | 78-78 | 1502 | 1496 | 56.5% | 1517 |
| Astros | 77-79 | 1493 | 1493 | 45.8% | 1481 |
There was some upheaval in the two division races represented in this tier. Entering last week one game behind the White Sox in the AL Central standings, the Guardians took two of three games against the South Siders in a dramatic series, which included a walk-off on Tuesday and an improbable go-ahead homer on Wednesday. From there, although Chicago took advantage of playing — and winning — on Thursday while Cleveland was off to pull back into a tie atop the division, the Guardians just kept winning, sweeping the the Athletics over the weekend to bring their winning streak to five. José Ramírez finally broke out of his extended slump, tallying nine hits, a home run, and four stolen bases last week.
As for the White Sox, they won three of their four games against the the Tigers, but that one loss was enough to drop them to a game behind Cleveland in the Central. Still, the Sox have a three-game cushion for the final AL Wild Card spot, and they own the tiebreaker over the Guardians, meaning both first place and a potential first-round bye are still in their sights. Miguel Vargas is carrying most of the load for the lineup right now, hitting three home runs last week, but he needs some support if Chicago wants to make some noise in the postseason.
Over in the AL West, the Astros were swept by the Braves this past weekend, allowing the Rangers to jump into first place with a .500 record. Texas enters this week one game up, but crucially Houston holds the tiebreaker. If the Rangers can manage to hang on, it would be just their second postseason appearance in the last decade. The last time they made the playoffs, they won the World Series.
The Houston bullpen was responsible for the backbreaking losses on Saturday and Sunday, but the lack of offense has been a much bigger problem. Over the Astros’ last 10 games, they’ve scored more than four runs in a game just once. Yordan Alvarez looked fine last week (eight hits, including two home runs) after his ankle scare the previous weekend, and Jeremy Peña has been great too (10 hits, three homers), but the rest of the lineup has been struggling. During this 10-game stretch, Houston hitters not named Alvarez or Peña have combined for an ugly 55 wRC+.
| Team | Record | Elo | Opponent Elo | Playoff Odds | Power Score |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Diamondbacks | 82-74 | 1527 | 1505 | 5.6% | 1464 |
| Blue Jays | 77-79 | 1516 | 1504 | 3.6% | 1456 |
The Diamondbacks managed to keep their slim playoff hopes alive with a pair of wins over the Yankees on Saturday and Sunday. The first victory was a walk-off and the second was highlighted by a go-ahead grand slam from Nolan Arenado. Arizona needs to take care of business in Colorado and get some help from the Dodgers to ensure that the final series against the Padres has some stakes. There’s a chance the Phillies could crash out, opening another window for the Snakes, but the direct path is through San Diego.
The Blue Jays’ hopes for a last-minute surge into the playoffs were dashed last week when they lost both of their series to the Tigers and Rangers. They’re three games back and have the Astros to contend with if they want to try and sneak into that final Wild Card spot. It’s probably too little, too late, but the team is activating Trey Yesavage off the IL on Monday as one more reinforcement ahead of a final push.

|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Pirates | 79-77 | 1534 | 1509 | 0.0% | 1465 |
| Mets | 71-85 | 1508 | 1509 | 0.0% | 1446 |
| Orioles | 75-81 | 1493 | 1504 | 0.1% | 1435 |

The series between the Orioles and Mets last week in Queens turned out to be more interesting than you’d expect from two teams mired in hugely disappointing seasons. Pete Alonso made his first appearance as a member of the opposing team at Citi Field and wound up hitting his 300th career home run on Tuesday, a game-tying shot in the ninth inning. He received a huge ovation from the hometown crowd, which drew some irksome comments from a few Mets players and staff after the game. Baltimore wound up sweeping New York to cut its deficit in the AL Wild Card race to 2.5 games. Alas, a sweep by the Brewers over the weekend slammed the door shut on any playoff hopes the O’s still had.
Even though the Marlins’ season essentially ended with that 12-game losing streak back in July, they have made some significant progress in their quest to become a contending club. Otto Lopez looks like a star they can build the lineup around, while Eury Pérez and Max Meyer should be strong enough to anchor the pitching staff in the years ahead. There’s also a cohort of young prospects in the upper minors who should be making their debuts soon. The future in Miami is brighter than it’s been in a while.
This is the huge step forward the Reds were hoping to see from Elly De La Cruz. In September, he has blasted seven home runs, including in five straight games earlier this month, and is running a major league-best 236 wRC+. It’s too bad the rest of Cincinnati’s roster is a bit of a mess. Sal Stewart has been excellent as De La Cruz’s sidekick, but the starting rotation has struggled mightily, and the big injury to Hunter Greene has thrown the ceiling of that group up in the air heading into next year. Still, building around a superstar like De La Cruz should make things easier if the resources to improve the rest of the roster are made available.

The AL Central crown runs through Kansas City; both the White Sox and Guardians travel to face the Royals during the final week of the season. Unfortunately, the Royals haven’t been playing well enough recently to act as a spoiler. They ended August with a 13-3 stretch, but they’ve been the worst team in the AL in September, with just five wins in 18 games.
It took a lot longer than expected, but the Twins were finally eliminated from the playoff race last week. It was a drama-filled week, too. They won a wild extra-inning walk-off affair against the Yankees on Wednesday and then were walked-off twice against the Angels between two shutout victories over the weekend. Even though they all made their big league debuts over the last few weeks, Walker Jenkins, Kaelen Culpepper, and Emmanuel Rodriguez never all appeared in a game together. That trio represents the future of the organization, so it’s a little disappointing that that future couldn’t be realized in a small way this year.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Spencer Jones is earning his spot on the postseason roster
item.dc:creator: Dani Mohr
item.description: Spencer Jones is finally gaining some momentum at the plate and earning his spot on the postseason roster after making some needed adjustments. Who does he have to thank, you might ask? Aaron Judge's hitting coach, perhaps. Jones, whose height and build are very similar to the Yankees captain, first met with Judge's hitting coach, Richard Schenk, during the offseason to make adjustments to his stance. item.content:encoded:
Spencer Jones is finally gaining some momentum at the plate and earning his spot on the postseason roster after making some needed adjustments. Who does he have to thank, you might ask?
Aaron Judge's hitting coach, perhaps.
Jones, whose height and build are very similar to the Yankees captain, first met with Judge's hitting coach, Richard Schenk, during the offseason to make adjustments to his stance. Although he may still struggle with frequent strikeouts, Jones is making a lot of positive progress that has helped him earn his place on this team.
The 25-year-old outfielder is hitting a .279 average with a .343 on-base percentage and .475 slugging percentage in September. Among Yankees, his .819 OPS and 130 wRC+ for the month are topped only by Ben Rice and Cody Bellinger, helping boost a Bombers lineup that sagged in August. After dealing with a sore left foot that kept him sidelined on Saturday, Jones returned to the lineup prepared to make some noise and launched a 448-foot homer off Corbin Burnes during the series finale against the Diamondbacks.
With Grisham still recovering from a right hamstring strain, Jones will be a valuable asset in the outfield—be it in center or right—who adds some depth to the lineup as well. It's also worth noting that Aaron Judge, who joined the IL on Friday with a right calf strain, will likely be sidelined for the beginning of the playoff run. As long as Jones can focus on developing his swing through these critical postseason at-bats, he has the potential to help the Yankees go far.
Beginning tomorrow afternoon, the Yankees will face the Rays in a critical four-game series that will ultimately determine the division and could even serve as a playoff preview. If he can stay consistent with his offensive production, Jones might just be the secret the Pinstripes need to seize the American League.
