item.content:encoded:
Although Aaron Judge intends to return from injury for the MLB postseason, it remains to be seen whether that will actually be possible. Aaron Boone and the New York Yankees have kept fans concerned about Judge’s injury, and a new report may all but confirm the worst-case scenario unfolding right before the Bronx Bombers’ eyes.
As things stand, neither party involved will reveal the grade of Judge‘s calf strain. That piece of information really isn’t too difficult to determine in today’s medicine and sports science landscape. Silence speaks volumes, though, and Judge, Boone, and the Yankees’ silence is loud enough to be heard all across the Big Apple.
“There’s no way [the Yankees] don’t know the grade [of Judge’s calf strain], it’s scientific data. The doctors don’t withhold it. They just won’t tell us what grade the strain is. If it was Grade 1, they would tell us that, because that’s good news,” Jimmy O’Brien stated on Talkin’ Yanks podcast. “And if it’s Grade 2, that gives three-to-six week return to running. I’ve got to think Judge is out.“
The fact that the Yankees have yet to reveal the extent of Judge’s injury could be taken as confirmation on its own. There are many reasons why the Bronx Bombers would say if it were good news, and many others why they wouldn’t if the results came out discouraging. All things considered, no answer appears to be an answer, and one no one in the Bronx wants to hear, so maybe that’s why New York isn’t putting it out there.
Aaron Judge #99 of the New York Yankees at Chase Field.
NY Yankees must make a decision on Judge
The timing of Judge’s latest setback couldn’t be any worse. Of course, it was always a possibility when New York decided to activate him off the 60-day IL with no rehab assignment while entering such a crucial stage of the MLB season. Still, the team is being held to a high standard, as made clear when Boone challenged the Judge-less Yankees to sweep the Tampa Bay Rays in the upcoming four-game series that will decide the fate of the AL East division.
As for Judge, he will be sidelined for that series, perhaps still unaware, or unwilling to reveal, how serious his calf strain really is. Whether he will actually be back for the postseason remains uncertain, but the odds aren’t looking too good. As Judge returned from his first right-rib stress fracture, there was a risk of re-injury. There are now two re-injury risks, and the injury in his lower body is one that could have an even more disastrous fate.
“Also, if you rush [Judge] back, it’s an injury [in his] lower leg that leads to Achilles ruptures and that would put him out for a year,” O’Brien concluded. “Are you going to risk running [designated hitter] Judge out there, which means you lose Ben Rice or Luis Garcia? I don’t fully agree [that Judge should play if he can], because there’s also the risk that he can get hurt. I don’t know if he helps the team enough, because [if Judge plays as DH] your second-best hitter has [to be taken out].”
NY Yankees at a crossroads
By all accounts, the Yankees are in a tough spot dealing with Judge’s latest injury. Everything else appears to be taken care of going into the postseason, but the uncertainty around the team’s best player risks throwing everything overboard and essentially making a great season, with a Cy Young Award favorite, all in vain. That’s the way it is in the Bronx: it’s always World-Series-or-bust, and without Judge, the Yankees may not be able to end the 16-year drought.
The fact that the Bronx Bombers are keeping their cards close to the vest may only confirm that they are bluffing. They don’t really have an ace up their sleeve and may only extend their act for as long as they can before eventually folding.
Key takeaways
- Withholding severity details fuels concerns surrounding right fielder Aaron Judge’s status for the postseason.
- A 3-to-6 week return timeline accompanies Grade 2 strains, per Talkin’ Yanks podcast hosts.
- Four-game series against Tampa Bay will decide the AL East division fate.

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX -- Varias latas de cerveza fueron vaciadas sobre la cabeza de Aaron Judge mientras el capitán de los Yankees permanecía en el centro del clubhouse de visitantes en el Target Field la semana pasada, rodeado de compañeros eufóricos que celebraban la clasificación del club a la postemporada.
Judge entrecerró los ojos por el ardor y les advirtió a sus compañeros: “Me las van a pagar”.
Aun así, no pretenden que ésa sea su última celebración, pues tienen un firme control del primer puesto del Comodín de la Liga Americana y el título del Este de la Liga Americana todavía está en juego.
“Siempre es bueno cuando puedes celebrar esos momentos durante una temporada”, dijo el manager de los Yankees, Aaron Boone. “Mucha gente dedica mucho tiempo, esfuerzo y sudor. Obviamente, éste es apenas el primer paso de lo que esperamos sean muchos”.
Ahora que aseguraron su pase a la postemporada, ¿qué más les espera a los Yankees?
¿Cómo podría quedar el roster para la postemporada?
C: Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez 
1B: Luis García Jr., Paul Goldschmidt
2B: Jazz Chisholm Jr.
3B: Ryan McMahon, Amed Rosario
SS: George Lombard Jr., José Caballero
OF: Cody Bellinger, Trent Grisham, Spencer Jones, Heliot Ramos
BD: Ben Rice
LA: Gerrit Cole, Cam Schlittler, Max Fried
R: David Bednar, Paul Blackburn, Brent Headrick, Tim Hill, Clarke Schmidt, Michael Fulmer, John Schreiber, Will Warren, Carlos Rodón
Los Yankees utilizaron a 12 lanzadores y a 14 bateadores cuando recibieron a los Medias Rojas en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, así que partiremos de esa misma premisa para el 2026.
Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles contra Tampa Bay, mientras que Schlittler lo hará el jueves. Mirando hacia adelante, eso sugiere que Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Es posible que los Yankees estén alineando a Cole para abrir el Juego 1 y a Schlittler para el Juego 2. Hasta ahora, han preferido no decir mucho al respecto, salvo por la confirmación de Boone de que Cole realizará una apertura en la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Rodón podría estar en el bullpen para la serie. En nuestra proyección del roster lo tenemos activo, mientras que el dominicano Luis Gil y Ryan Yarbrough figuran entre quienes quedarían fuera. Ryan Weathers trabaja para regresar como relevista, pero el tiempo juega en su contra. Si está saludable, podría ocupar el lugar de Fulmer o Schreiber.
Chisholm espera regresar esta semana para la serie contra los Rays tras sufrir un esguince en el pulgar derecho, mientras que Grisham ha mostrado mejoría y podría quedarse con un puesto en los jardines. De no ser así, Max Schuemann está entre las alternativas. Otro aspecto para seguir: ¿Podrían los Yankees incluir a Anthony Volpe en lugar de Rosario? Es una posibilidad que vale la pena considerar.
¿Cuándo comenzará la postemporada?
Si los Yankees terminan disputando la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, ésta empezará el 29 de septiembre. La Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana arrancará el 3 de octubre.
¿Contra quién jugarían los Yankees si la temporada terminara hoy?
En estos momentos, sería una revancha de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana del año pasado, con los Yankees recibiendo a los Medias Rojas en el Bronx. Los Yankees ganaron aquella serie dos victorias por una.
Este año, los Yankees tuvieron marca de 7-6 contra Boston.
¿Todavía pueden ganar el Este de la Liga Americana?
Sí, pero tienen un camino cuesta arriba. Los Yankees tienen por delante cuatro enfrentamientos directos con los Rays a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium, incluyendo una doble-cartelera para abrir la serie. Tampa Bay domina actualmente la serie particular por 6-3, lo que significa que los Yankees necesitarían barrer para quedarse con el criterio de desempate entre ambos.
¿Quién abriría el Juego 1 por los Yankees?
Como se mencionó anteriormente, Cole está programado para lanzar el miércoles frente a Tampa Bay y Schlittler lo hará al día siguiente. Por lo tanto, Cole tendría un día adicional de descanso antes del Juego 1 de la Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana, mientras que Schlittler estaría con su descanso normal.
Después de permitir siete jonrones en sus dos aperturas anteriores, Cole mermó las dudas externas sobre una posible apertura en los playoffs con una sólida actuación en Arizona. Fried y Rodón han lidiado con lesiones, pero están recuperando su mejor nivel en el momento indicado.
Warren realizará una apertura más durante la serie contra los Orioles, según Boone, pero llegará a los playoffs como una interesante alternativa para el relevo.
¿Será Judge un factor en los playoffs?
Los Yankees han sido poco específicos sobre el estado de Judge. Boone ha evitado ofrecer un plazo estimado para su recuperación e incluso revelar el grado del tirón en la pantorrilla derecha. En términos generales, hasta un tirón de Grado 1, el de menor gravedad, requiere de dos a tres semanas para una recuperación completa.
Es casi seguro que Judge intentará regresar antes. La primera fecha en la que podría ser activado sería para el Juego 162, el 27 de septiembre. Tal como está el panorama ahora mismo, existe una posibilidad muy real de que los Yankees no cuenten con Judge al menos para una potencial Serie del Comodín de la Liga Americana.
Judge dijo que le “gustaría” estar activo para la postemporada y que ése es “el plan”, pero no dijo necesariamente que sería para el 29 de septiembre.
¿Cuáles son las otras preocupaciones en cuanto a lesiones?
Grisham ha avanzado en su programa progresivo de correr y debe de estar disponible para el roster de los playoffs, aunque Boone dijo que no será activado antes de que termine la temporada regular. Chisholm ha estado bateando y realizando tiros, y debe de ser activado durante la serie contra los Rays. Si sufre algún contratiempo, Volpe entraría en consideración.
Y aunque los Yankees no han descartado a Giancarlo Stanton, quien ha estado bateando, han ofrecido pocas novedades sobre su recuperación del más reciente tirón en la pantorrilla.

item.content:encoded:
You know that the Pittsburgh Pirates’ offseason has officially arrived when we’re talking about a potential Paul Skenes trade.
It’s been a bit, hasn’t it? The Pirates remained in NL Wild Card contention throughout the second half, which ordinarily would be enough to halt the annual speculation. But Skenes has looked nothing like his Cy Young self, and he could realistically end the year with an ERA above 4.00. This is the same pitcher who had a 1.96 ERA through his first 320.2 innings and looked unhittable most nights.
In the grand scheme of things, nothing has changed. Skenes hasn’t publicly requested a trade, and the Pirates have insisted they won’t trade the three-time All-Star. Objectively, we imagine he’ll be toeing the mound on Opening Day 2027, whenever that might be.
Bleacher Report’s Zachary D. Rymer nonetheless pitched (pun intended) two possible Skenes trades, one involving the Yankees and another featuring Mets. Needless to say, we have plenty of thoughts.
Yankees send Ben Rice, Spencer Jones, and two pitchers to the Pirates for Paul Skenes and Bryan Reynolds
Pirates grade: C+
Yankees grade: C-
Those who spend much of their free time scrolling X/Twitter (hey, we know the feeling all too well) are likely familiar with the meme of Bugs Bunny squinting his eyes and saying “No.” That’s exactly how we felt upon initially seeing this trade offer.
Let’s start with the obvious: the Yankees aren’t trading Rice. At no point did we hear his name floated amid the Tarik Skubal rumors, and his left-handed power makes him a perfect fit for Yankee Stadium’s short porch. He’ll either open next season as the starting first baseman or designated hitter, depending on what Giancarlo Stanton’s future looks like; the 2017 NL MVP has one year left on his deal, and he’s been an injury liability since the start of 2019.
We’re skeptical that Jones would be moved unless the return involves an MVP-caliber outfielder. Trent Grisham is a pending free agent, and we’re genuinely unsure what Jasson Domínguez’s future in New York looks like, especially after his recent demotion to Triple-A. When a team doesn’t want you on the big-league roster ahead of the playoffs, what does that say?
Reynolds has had a fine year, and he entered Sunday leading the league in doubles. But if you’re the Yankees, do you really want to give up Jones and Lagrange for an outfielder who turns 32 in January? Reynolds is under contract through 2030 (with a $20 million team option for 2031), and that’s a significant commitment to someone who, at his best, is a mid-3 bWAR player.
We must also note that Rymer claimed that Rodríguez ranked No. 82 and Lagrange placed No. 100 on MLB Pipeline, which is simply untrue. Shortstop Dax Kilby is the only Yankees player on the most recent MLB Pipeline list, and he placed No. 83. So the Pirates wouldn’t even be landing a top-100 prospect? Hard pass.
That said, we’ll give the Yankees a C- for their return, because an elite Skenes ranks among the game’s best pitchers. But will we see him regain that 2024-25 form? That we’re even asking the question should say enough.
Mets give up Carson Benge and two prospects for Pirates teammates Paul Skenes and Bryan Reynolds
Pirates grade: D
Mets grade: C
At least the proposed Pirates-Yankees trade made some sense. We can’t say the same about Pittsburgh theoretically shipping Skenes and Reynolds to the Mets for Benge, Rojas, and Tong.
First off, why would the Mets only need to give up three players rather than the Yankees’ four? Rymer listed Rojas as the No. 79 prospect and Tong at No. 88, neither of which is accurate; Rojas is No. 73, and MLB Pipeline no longer lists Tong among its top 100 prospects, for reasons we don’t understand. Mariners lefty Kade Anderson has thrown 25.1 big-league innings, and he's still ranked No. 5, but Tong and his 39.2 innings over two seasons no longer qualify. Huh?
Benge has quietly enjoyed a solid rookie season, hitting .276 with 19 home runs, 61 RBIs, 22 steals, and a .760 OPS through his first 149 games. But for him to be the centerpiece of a deal involving both Skenes and Reynolds is absurd. Oh, and Benge turns 24 in January, so he’d be a slightly older second-year starter.
As for the Mets, adding yet another long-term contract isn’t the answer to putting their disastrous 2026 season behind them. As we’ve said before, Bo Bichette would be foolish to exercise his opt-out clause and leave $42 million in guaranteed money on the table. Marcus Semien has two years and $46 million left on his deal, and we’re not even factoring in Francisco Lindor’s contract.
That said, we’ve seen enough positives from Benge thus far to hold off on giving the Pirates’ theoretical return an “F” grade. But both teams should pass on even contemplating such an offer.

September 21 Notes
Falling off: Aaron Judge (ninth), Dylan Cease (40th), Alex Bregman (43rd), Andrés Muñoz (71st), Jesús Luzardo (93rd), Troy Melton (117th), Bryce Eldridge (140th) and 36 other players.
- It’s a fool’s errand, but here’s one last update for the final week of the season. I tried emphasizing two-start starters unless they’re particularly dangerous, but I also tried to take into account that some of the guys currently in line to start twice are going to end up being scratched or making only brief appearances next weekend.
- With no updates yet on Alex Bregman (face) and Andrés Muñoz (knee), I’ve dropped both from the rankings. Pedro Ramírez, who was set to fall off the list with Dansby Swanson back, reclaimed a spot in Bregman’s place. Seranthony Domínguez seems like the likeliest choice for saves in Seattle in Muñoz’s place, so he comes in at No. 166.
- Thank you so much to everyone who has followed along all season. Anyone interested in the full spreadsheet of where players have ranked start to finish, reach out to my gmail at matthewpouliot. I’ll be back in mid-October with the first (or second) go at a 2027 Top 300.
September 14 Notes
Falling off: Shohei Ohtani DH (eighth), Rafael Devers (41st), Jazz Chisholm Jr. (58th), Bryce Miller (177th), Gleyber Torres (183rd), Hayden Wesneski (206th), Royce Lewis (214th), Kyle Bradish (222nd), Michael McGreevy (243rd), Brandon Pfaadt (246th), Braxton Ashcraft (250th) and 21 other players
- I don’t have much of a notes section for you right now, since it’s after 3 am and I’d like to get some sleep. Still, the rankings are updated for the final 14 days of the season. A lot of the pitcher movement this week is elevating guys with three starts remaining and dropping those with only two. I also gave Rockies hitters a nice boost, as they play 10 of their remaining 13 games at home. Padres hitters also got a little lift from that, as they’ll be starting a four-game series in Coors Field on Monday.
September 7 Notes
Falling off: Kyle Harrison (101st), Shane McClanahan (125th), Luis Robert Jr. (163rd), Trent Graham (180th), Joe Musgrove (192nd), Byron Buxton (202nd), Cam Smith (219th), Brendan Donovan (227th), JJ Wetherholt (236th), Eric Lauer (243rd), Jesús Sánchez (247th), Xavier Edwards (254th), Sean Manaea (261st), Samuel Basallo (262nd), Nathan Eovaldi (265th), Connor Norby (268th), Chase Burns (273rd), Shohei Ohtani SP (280th), Tommy White (282nd), Daniel Palencia (285th), Colton Cowser (286th), Taylor Ward (289th), Ezequiel Tovar (290th), Alek Thomas (292nd), Willi Castro (294th), Elvis Alvarado (295th), Brandyn Garcia (299th)
- With three weeks to go, nearly every injured player is off the rankings at this point, with the exception of a few guys hopefully returning before the end of this week. Also, I’m paying a lot more attention to matchups, particularly this week’s. So, some starters with multiple starts this week who wouldn’t normally be in the top 300 make the cut. Also, Athletics hitters have moved up, since they’ll be at home for six games this week. Rockies hitters have dropped off as that team goes back on the road after a week of home games.
- Rafael Devers gets an overdue late bump. There really was good reason for concern early on with his strikeout rate up and his bat speed down, but he bounced back nicely in both categories. Amazing is the consistency in his wOBAs since 2021: .373, .373, .359, .364, .365 and .365. His xwOBAs, on the other hand, still show a little decline: .391, .365, .380, .366, .367, .340. Still, it’s been a really impressive season, and getting to 100 runs scored (maybe) and 100 RBI (almost certainly) on the moribund Giants offense is one heck of an accomplishment.
- The Orioles getting swept by Red Sox over the weekend, dropping their postseason odds at Fangraphs to just three percent, would seem to greatly increase the chances that Kyle Bradish gets shut down with a week or two to go. He’s up to 152 innings in his first full year back from Tommy John, and he’s not exactly doing his best work at the moment.
- Kyle Harrison might have lost his rotation spot with his performance Sunday against the Reds, though I thought about keeping him on the list anyway, since he could be well set up for wins in middle relief if moved to the pen. In the end, he didn’t quite make the cut. It will be really interesting to see how the Brewers play things the rest of the way. I imagine both Jacob Misiorowski and Logan Henderson will make a couple of shorter starts in an attempt to save bullets for October.
- It’ll be nice to see Corbin Burnes back on a major league mound Tuesday, but given that he threw just two innings in his lone rehab start after Tommy John, so I couldn’t see including him here just yet. San Diego’s Nick Pivetta, on the other hand, at least made it up to 4 1/3 innings in his last rehab start as he returns from an elbow injury. That gets him a spot on the bottom of the list, even if he’s a long shot to get a win Monday in his return.

item.title: [MLB.com] With AL East title on line, Yanks determined to keep Rays from celebrating in Bronx
item.dc:creator: Bryan Hoch; Adam Berry

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK -- It has felt inevitable that the American League East race would be decided this week in the Bronx.
The Rays have led the Majors’ most competitive division for most of the season, and they haven’t ceded the top spot in the standings since reclaiming first place on June 27.
But the Yankees have always been there -- threatening and falling back, perhaps -- but never trailing by enough to diminish the potential importance of this week.
Well, here it is.
The Yankees will host the Rays in a four-game series at Yankee Stadium, beginning with a separate-admission doubleheader on Tuesday. Thanks to the Rays’ terrific homestand and the Yankees’ series loss in Phoenix, the question now is how much longer this race will remain alive.
The Rays arrived in New York holding a six-game lead in the division race with only seven games remaining. One victory by Tampa Bay will eliminate the Yankees from the AL East race and lock them into an AL Wild Card spot. So for the Yankees to have any chance, they must pull off a four-game, three-day sweep.
The stakes? As Gerrit Cole once said, “They’re high.” Let’s dive in.
What’s at stake?
Rays: Winning just one game will guarantee the Rays’ first AL East championship since 2021, giving them a bye through the Wild Card Series and home field advantage in both the AL Division Series and -- if they advance -- the AL Championship Series. They also need just one win to clinch the season series against the Yankees.
Yankees: Manager Aaron Boone acknowledges that it would be a “tall order” to keep the Rays from spraying bubbly in the Bronx, but that’s exactly what they intend to do. They entered the season looking to change the narrative after coming up short in their pursuit of the Blue Jays last year. They’re instead on the verge of settling for another consolation prize and needing to fight through a best-of-three.
How are the starting rotations lined up?
Rays: They will send their two best starters to the mound for Tuesday’s doubleheader. First comes veteran right-hander Nick Martinez, their clubhouse leader and most dependable source of innings. Tampa Bay has a 22-7 record behind Martinez this season. Then comes Drew Rasmussen, one of the AL’s top starters. The Rays haven’t lost one of Rasmussen’s starts since July 9, going a perfect 11-0 in his outings since then. Martinez will be pitching with an extra day of rest, while Rasmussen will be working on four days’ rest for only the seventh time this season. Left-hander Ian Seymour and right-hander Freddy Peralta would be in line to start Wednesday and Thursday, respectively.
Yankees: Carlos Rodón and Max Fried will start the doubleheader, in that order. Both have dealt with injuries this season but are rounding into form at the right time. In three September starts, Rodón is 2-0 with a 2.08 ERA, putting a bout with left elbow inflammation into his rear-view mirror. After twice landing on the injured list with a bone bruise in his pitching elbow, Fried is 1-0 with a 1.69 ERA in three September starts. Cole and AL Cy Young Award frontrunner Cam Schlittler follow in the third and fourth games of the series, respectively.
What has been going well for each team lately?
Rays: Um, everything? The Rays just went 8-1 during their final regular-season homestand, and they’ve won four straight series against the Braves, Astros, A’s and Red Sox. Since getting swept in a four-game series at Fenway Park coming out of the All-Star break, they’ve put together a 39-18 record -- the best in baseball since July 20. Their starting pitching has been particularly strong, with a 2.81 ERA this month that ranks second to only the Yankees. They have found different ways to score runs, as usual, including early rallies like Sunday and a pair of walk-off homers from AL MVP candidate Junior Caminero.
Yankees: These Yanks suddenly find themselves leaning on the strength of their pitching, believing the offense will eventually deliver. Ben Rice cracked his team-leading 39th home run, fulfilling a prediction Boone made in Spring Training. Rice said Boone was teasing him, coming up “one or two” short of his preferred total, so look for Rice to swing for his 40th this week. Austin Wells has hit three homers in his last six games, while Heliot Ramos has homered in his last two games. He could be an important piece if the Yankees are going to make October noise.
What are some areas of concern that could be an issue this week or in the postseason?
Rays: Plenty of Rays have picked up the slack, but leadoff man Yandy Díaz has had a tough month, with a .229/.286/.357 slash line in September. He sets the tone for their lineup, so it’s obviously important for him to be in top form come October. And this is really nitpicking, considering he’s 3-0 with a save and a 1.42 ERA this month, but MLB saves leader Bryan Baker has more walks (four) than strikeouts (two) in seven September appearances. He’ll need to be lights-out in the postseason, too.
Yankees: Other than Aaron Judge’s right calf strain, which the Yankees are treating like a top-secret matter of national importance, there are concerns bubbling about the state of the bullpen. Brent Headrick’s velocity has dipped and he may be showing fatigue after a Major League-leading 79 appearances. Tim Hill hasn’t been the automatic ground-ball machine of years past. Michael Fulmer gave up a game-winning homer in Arizona. But there’s no bigger issue than proving they can win without Judge, the engine around which their offense is built. They are 48-41 without him, compared to 41-25 with him.

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Aaron Judge injury explained: What is Yankees star facing? Surgeon talks possible return, risk
item.dc:creator: Randy Miller

item.content:encoded:
NEW YORK — The Yankees surely were in a somber mood during Sunday night's cross-country flight from Phoenix to New York. The AL East race is all but over and Aaron Judge is hurt again, this time potentially for the season.
The Diamondbacks prevailed 5-3 on Saturday night and 8-4 on Sunday afternoon, costing the Yankees two more games in the standings and leaving them six games behind with seven games remaining in the regular season.
Following Monday's off day, the first-place Rays will be in the Bronx for four games in three days at Yankee Stadium, which will probably lead to champagne corks popping in the visiting clubhouse. The Rays need just one win to clinch the AL East.
At this point, the Yankees will inevitably face the Red Sox a week from Tuesday in Game 1 of a Wild Card Series.
The mystery is whether Judge will be back for this best-of-three.
Here's what we know:
1. The three-time MVP is back on the injured list with a right calf strain less than two weeks after returning from a fractured rib that sidelined him for 88 games.
2. The strain is in the soleus muscle.
3. He's eligible to be activated for next Sunday's regular-season finale, game 162.
How bad is it? What did the MRI reveal?
As usual, the Yankees and Judge have remained guarded/secretive about revealing his injury and rehab details.
"It doesn't matter what the grade is," manager Aaron Boone said last Friday in Phoenix. "We're going to get him back or we're not. That's what we're going to work to do and we'll see.''
Judge basically said the same thing to Yankees media on Saturday, while adding, "I'd like to be back for the playoffs. That's definitely the plan."
What can we unpack from what little we know?
NJ.com consulted with an NYU Langone Health sports orthopedic surgeon to provide a clearer picture of what Judge is facing without knowing if the strain is a Grade 1 (mild), Grade 2 (moderate partial tear) or Grade 3 (severe complete rupture).
"If it's a Grade 1, in two weeks you could see Judge doing baseball activities again and then three weeks back playing," Dr. Spencer Stein said. "It's a calf muscle strain and they're annoying injuries."
Judge was injured during last Wednesday's game in Minnesota, so three weeks would be Oct. 7. If the Yankees win their Wild Card Series, that would be Game 3 of their best-of-five Division Series with the Rays.
"But that's really best-case scenario," Dr. Stein said. "That would be the fastest."
Yankees designated hitter Giancarlo Stanton went on the IL in April with a Grade 1 calf strain and still hasn't returned. He had a setback in June, and then while rehabbing, he strained his other calf in August.
If Judge rushes back, he'd also be risking a setback, the doctor warned.
"I've seen studies there's up to 50% chance of re-injury in these muscular injuries — hamstring injuries, calf muscle injuries," Dr. Stein said. "There's a high rate of retear, so it's definitely a balance of not going back too quickly on them."
Rushing back might be why Judge is hurt again. When he was out with his rib injury, he was shut down from baseball activities from June 1 until Aug. 19. Less than three weeks later, Judge was back from the IL and playing right field for the Yankees with no rehab games and a few live batting-practice at-bats packed into a workout the day before his first game back.
"Well, I would say that there should always be a stepwise return to sports where you build things up and that takes time," Dr. Stein said. "When you're under a time constraint because it's end of season and the playoffs are around the corner, sometimes you have to take a risk and go a little faster. But with a risk, you can end up with another injury."
The location of his calf strain is problematic.
"The gastrocnemius, plantaris and soleus muscles comprise the calf, and the soleus muscle is a push-off muscle and part of the Achilles tendon," Dr. Stein said. "There's just a lot of force in that area, a lot of strain and stress, especially when you're swinging a baseball bat."
If Judge returns, he'd be much better off DHing instead of playing right field, Dr. Stein added.
"No question," he said. "The soleus muscle constantly is engaged during simple standing and walking."
That's another risk the Yankees would have to take.
Judge would have to play right field rather than be the designated hitter. Ben Rice, who has 39 home runs and 95 RBI, is entrenched at DH, while Luis Garcia Jr. and Paul Goldschmidt form a potent first base first-base platoon
Here is Dr. Stein's advice for Judge:
"Follow the instructions and take it day-by-day. Work with the therapists and trainers. Make sure your strength is there. You don't want to rush it too much. You don't want a long-term injury that keeps happening.
"You want to be able to come back, and we get that, but you do want to meet the criteria: Good strength with a good amount of flexibility in the knee and ankle area."
Read the original article on NJ.com. Add NJ.com as a Preferred Source by clicking here.

item.title: [New York Daily News] Yankees playoff roster prediction: Who makes the cut with division dreams dwindling ahead of Rays series?
item.dc:creator: Gary Phillips

Unable to bounce back with an 8-4 loss in Sunday’s series finale against Arizona, the second-place Yankees are now six games back of the division-leading Rays with seven games left in the regular season. The rivals will play four of those games against each other
item.content:encoded:
Shortly after getting walked-off by the Diamondbacks on Saturday night, the Yankees acknowledged their reality.
“Mathematically, [it’s] probably pretty tough, but you never know,” Cody Bellinger said of winning the American League East.
Unable to bounce back with an 8-4 loss in Sunday’s series finale against Arizona, the second-place Yankees are now six games back of the division-leading Rays with seven games left in the regular season. The rivals will play four of those games against each other at Yankee Stadium this week, starting with a doubleheader on Tuesday.
Aaron Boone acknowledged that his team will probably have to sweep the Rays just for a crack at the division crown, as FanGraphs gave the Yankees a measly 2.7% chance of winning the AL East before Sunday’s game.
“There’s still a chance,” Cam Schlittler said, “but we gotta play our asses off a little bit.”
While the Yankees still technically have a shot to defy the odds, the far likelier scenario is that their postseason begins on Sept. 29 at home against Boston in the Wild Card round for the second straight year.
With that in mind, let’s try to predict what the club’s roster could look like for that series.
Hitters (15): Ben Rice, Heliot Ramos, Spencer Jones, Trent Grisham, Cody Bellinger, Ryan McMahon, George Lombard Jr., Paul Goldschmidt, Luis García Jr., Jazz Chisholm Jr., José Caballero, Austin Wells, Ali Sánchez, Anthony Volpe, Amed Rosario
With the Yankees providing minimal info on Aaron Judge’s calf strain, it can’t be assumed he’ll be available.
Jazz Chisholm Jr. could return from a sprained thumb as soon as Tuesday. Meanwhile, Trent Grisham is still in play as a playoff option as he recovers from a hamstring strain, but Boone said that activating him before the end of the regular season is “complicated,” partly due to roster logistics.
With Max Schuemann presumably the corresponding move for Chisholm, the Yankees would have to option someone else if they activated Grisham before the playoffs. That someone wouldn’t be able to be recalled for 10 days barring a new injury; it seems like Jasson Domínguez is being protected from that window in case he’s needed for the Wild Card roster.
Grisham has been doing baseball activities and is “pretty deep into his running progression,” Boone said. If he is on the Wild Card roster, the Yankees will have an interesting decision to make between him and Spencer Jones in center field.
Third base could also be a conundrum, as Ryan McMahon and José Caballero don’t offer much offensively, and Amed Rosario is a poor defender. He’s only on the roster as an option against lefties, even though he hasn’t been great against them.
Another idea would be to use Volpe, who has been playing second, at third against lefties since he played a few games there in the minors this season. However, he doesn’t have a strong arm, and he hasn’t been working at third base since being recalled. Volpe said that the Yankees have not talked to him about manning the hot corner before the regular season ends.
“We’ll see,” Boone said. “First things first, getting Jazz back, and then we’ll figure out as the week unfolds how I want to play it.”
Volpe can also play second over Chisholm against lefties.
Pitchers (11): Cam Schlittler, Gerrit Cole, Max Fried, Will Warren, David Bednar, Brent Headrick, Paul Blackburn, Clarke Schmidt, John Schreiber, Tim Hill, Ryan Weathers
As things stand, Carlos Rodón, Max Fried, Gerrit Cole and Cam Schlittler are scheduled to pitch against the Rays, in that order. That would give Cole, who has struggled to get swing-and-miss, an extra day of rest if he were to start Game 1 of the Wild Card round. Schlittler, the AL Cy Young frontrunner, would be on regular rest if tabbed for Game 1.
Because the Wild Card round is a best-of-three series, Rodón isn’t needed, especially with Will Warren expected to work out of the bullpen and able to provide length.
Warren, slated to make one more start this season after struggling on Sunday, is one of a few converted starters who could impact the Bombers’ bullpen this postseason. Clarke Schmidt and Ryan Weathers are the others. Schmidt, being cautious in his return from Tommy John surgery, couldn’t come into Sunday’s game due to some bicep cramping, while Weathers isn’t expected to return from a flexor strain before the regular season ends.
Still, neither Boone nor pitching coach Matt Blake ruled out the idea of Weathers’ first game back coming in the playoffs.
“I don’t know if ‘comfortable’ is [the right word],” Blake said, “but it might be the course of action where he’s the best option even though he hasn’t pitched in the last three or four weeks.”
As for the relievers that the Yankees have leaned on all season, David Bednar, Paul Blackburn and Brent Headrick headline the group. All have been used heavily, especially Headrick.
The lefty allowed a grand slam to Nolan Arenado and saw his fastball velocity down an average of 1.3 mph during his major league-leading 79th appearance on Sunday, but he insisted that he feels fine physically. Boone also downplayed concerns over Headrick’s ongoing velocity fluctuations, though he did say that he hopes to get him and other relievers “in a good spot” with some rest ahead of the playoffs.
That said, the Yankees still haven’t been eliminated from the AL East race. They’ll keep trying to take the division from the Rays until they are.
“We’re going to show up Tuesday,” Boone said, “and try and kick their butt.”

item.content:encoded:
Despite landing on the injured list, Aaron Judge is still eager to contribute to the Yankees in the postseason.
Judge, who chose to forgo a rehab assignment in favor of rejoining the team earlier in the month, told the media that he wanted to recover from his right calf strain by the start of postseason play. The American League Wild Card Series, which the Yankees would play in if the season ended today, is slated to begin on Sept. 29, just 10 days from now.
On Saturday, Judge offered a simple "we'll see" when asked if he'd be back in time for the playoff action (h/t Brendan Kuty).
So if Judge were to return before then, his stay on the injured list would effectively last a minimum of 10 days. Unfortunately, it's highly unlikely that he fully recovers by then—and from a team perspective, it's not worth it for the Yankees to rush him back.
The Yankees' best lineup needs Judge in the outfield
Judge's injury will effectively prevent him from playing in right field and limit him to designated hitter duties. However, the Yankees' best lineup needs him playing in right field, as sticking him at DH with the roster currently constructed will force another one of the team's best hitters onto the bench.
After spending the first half of the season as the Yankees' starting first baseman, Ben Rice became the everyday DH when the team traded for Luis Garcia Jr., who subsequently took over at first. Garcia plays much better defense at first than Rice does, but Rice has been more productive overall (h/t Yankees) at the plate.
Regardless, both are among the Yankees' best hitters and will be integral to their postseason run.
By having Judge at DH, either Garcia or Rice would come out of the lineup. If Rice is playing first, the Yankees lose access to Garcia's strong glove at the position as well as a threat for extra bases in the heart of the order. If Garcia is at first, the team loses access to Rice's elite power and outstanding poise in clutch situations.
If one of them is called upon to pinch-hit at any point, then one will take over for the other for the rest of the game.
Having Judge in right field instead of the DH spot allows the Yankees to play both Garcia and Rice. But putting Judge in the field with a bad calf is a recipe for disaster.
The Yankees can't afford a career-altering injury to Judge
Calf strains are notorious for being easy to re-injure; look no further than Giancarlo Stanton, who essentially missed the entire season due to calf strains in both legs, including a re-injury to the original strain when rehabbing.
The calf also leads into the Achilles tendon, which becomes vulnerable to tears if the calf is already injured. Achilles tears are not only season-ending in any sport, but the long-term effects are devastating. In a baseball example, former Phillies first baseman Ryan Howard was one of the game's premier sluggers before an Achilles tear during the 2011 postseason, and he was never the same hitter after.
The Yankees don't want that for Judge, and neither does he (h/t Gary Phillips).
If Judge were to reaggravate the calf or tear his Achilles, he risks missing even more time during the 2027 season. The Yankees already saw how dramatically the offense struggles when he's out long-term, and they simply can't risk that happening again next year, especially for a player approaching his mid-30s. Neither Judge nor the Yankees even know the grade of the calf strain right now, which is further reason not to chance anything and shut him down.
Obviously, Judge still wants to play during the postseason because that's when the games matter the most. But given the nature of his injury—which is to the soleus muscle, a crucial part of his ability to hit and run—playing through it isn't an option.
The only option is for the rest of the team to step up in Judge's absence and make a deep postseason run, and perhaps the Yankees can get their captain back if he's feeling 100% by the AL Championship Series or World Series.
Joe Najarian is a writer for Yankees On SI, having previously covered the Yankees both for SI and additional sites since 2023. He also served as Deputy Editor for the Yankees, Mets and Orioles On SI sites, and additionally contributes to Athlon Sports and Men’s Journal covering Major League Baseball and other trending sports news. Joe is a graduate of Rutgers University in 2022, earning a bachelor’s degree in Journalism and Media Studies.
Follow JoeNajarian

item.content:encoded:
The Colorado Rockies are 57–99.
Purple Row After Dark: If the Rockies could steal one player
An absurd rule for absurd times: if the worst team in baseball could steal one player from a playoff club, who should the Rockies take?
One more loss will give them their fourth consecutive 100-loss season, and they are almost certainly going to finish with the worst record in baseball.
These are absurd times for the Rockies, so I have devised an appropriately absurd rule to help them out.
The team with the worst record in baseball gets to steal one player from a playoff team.
There are, naturally, some restrictions. We’re freezing the playoff field as it stood before games on Sunday, September 20. The player has to come from one of those 12 teams, cannot be a pending free agent, and you cannot take the player who leads his team in FanGraphs WAR. The Rockies also inherit the player’s existing contract.
No, one player is not suddenly turning the Rockies into a contender. But could one poached superstar at least keep this thing from becoming five consecutive 100-loss seasons?
Here’s the board:
| Team | Off limits: fWAR leader | Highest available fWAR | Other players worth considering |
| Rays | Junior Caminero (5.2) | Drew Rasmussen (4.7) | Jonathan Aranda (3) |
| Guardians | Parker Messick (4.6) | Steven Kwan (3.4) | Gavin Williams (3.4), Brayan Rocchio (3.3), José Ramírez (2.2) |
| Rangers | Ezequiel Duran (4.6) | Jacob deGrom (4.2) | Josh Jung (2.9), Wyatt Langford (2.8) |
| Yankees | Cam Schlittler (6.1) | Ben Rice (4) | Cody Bellinger (3.9), Aaron Judge (2) |
| Red Sox | Willson Contreras (4.1) | Payton Tolle (4) | Ceddanne Rafaela (3.9), Ranger Suárez (3.7) |
| White Sox | Miguel Vargas (5) | Chase Meidroth (4) | Tristan Peters (3.9), Sean Burke (3.1) |
| Brewers | Jacob Misiorowski (6.3) | Brice Turang (5.4) | Jackson Chourio (4), Jake Bauers (3.6) |
| Dodgers | Shohei Ohtani (6.7) | Yoshinobu Yamamoto (4.7) | Max Muncy (4.3), Andy Pages (3.9) |
| Braves | Chris Sale (5.7) | Michael Harris II (4) | Matt Olson (4), Drake Baldwin (3.1) |
| Cubs | Pete Crow-Armstrong (10.2) | Alex Bregman (5) | Dansby Swanson (3.6) |
| Padres | Fernando Tatis Jr. (5) | Jackson Merrill (4) | Ty France (3.8), Mason Miller (3.7) |
| Phillies | Cristopher Sánchez (5.8) | Jesús Luzardo (5.6) | Zack Wheeler (3.5), Bryce Harper (3.4) |
For me, the choice comes down to Brice Turang, Yoshinobu Yamamoto and Aaron Judge.
Turang is probably the sensible choice.
At 5.4 fWAR, he would easily lead the Rockies, giving them a legitimate top-end player while immediately solving second base for the foreseeable future. He’s 26, hitting .266/.367/.441 with an .808 OPS, and brings value on both sides of the ball with elite range, strong baserunning and a 95th-percentile walk rate.
It would be a very easy way to make the roster better.
But the Rockies really need starting pitching.
Enter Yoshinobu Yamamoto.
He’s 14–8 with a 2.51 ERA, 178 strikeouts and a 0.87 WHIP over 179 innings. His Statcast profile is just as impressive: 100th-percentile pitching run value, 99th-percentile fastball run value, 95th-percentile offspeed run value and a 91st-percentile xERA.
Pitchers are risky, and Yamamoto comes with a lot of money attached. But it’s hard to argue with either the profile or the results, and the addition of the Penner family makes absorbing that contract a lot easier to imagine.
Speaking of high-priced items...
Aaron Judge.
Judge being available is basically a loophole created by our own stupid rule. Injuries have limited him to just 285 plate appearances, which is why he sits at only 2 fWAR, but he’s still hitting .241/.360/.511 with 15 home runs.
And the underlying numbers are still very much Judge: a .396 xwOBA, .569 xSLG, 94.0 mph average exit velocity and a 57.5% hard-hit rate.
It is very hard to look at that and say, “No thanks.”
After all, Aaron Judge is the type of hitter that, if he were playing 81 games a year at Coors Field, I might take out a small loan for season tickets.
So who are you stealing?

item.title: [Yahoo Sports] Yankees' Paul Goldschmidt Has Gone From Disposable to Indispensable
item.dc:creator: Matthew Schmidt
item.description: For a short while there, it appeared that Paul Goldschmidt was a prime candidate to be left off the New York Yankees' postseason roster. item.content:encoded:
For a short while there, it appeared that Paul Goldschmidt was a prime candidate to be left off the New York Yankees' postseason roster.
The addition of Luis Garcia Jr. had completely clouded Goldschmidt's role, and it appeared that the impending returns of Aaron Judge and Giancarlo Stanton would make the former NL MVP rather disposable.
My, how things have changed.
Yes, Goldschmidt's at-bats have still been somewhat sparse since the arrival of Garcia at the MLB trade deadline, but with Judge and Stanton now both potentially out for the playoffs (or at least the Wild Card Series), Goldschmidt's value just increased exponentially.
Suddenly, Goldschmidt is now one of the Yankees' very best options against left-handed pitching, and he may get some starts in the playoffs now that Judge and Stanton are both on the shelf.
Goldschmidt has always mashed southpaws, owning a lifetime 1.006 OPS against them. This year, he is slashing .309/.404/.592 versus lefties, making him a must on New York's playoff squad.
It should also be noted that after a miserable month of July and after barely playing in August, Goldschmidt has gone 6-for-18 at the plate this month, so he is starting to rediscover his stroke as October draws near.
And with the Boston Red Sox — New York's likely Wild Card opponent — being loaded with left-handers, Goldschmidt will likely get significant playing time early on in the postseason.
In that scenario, Ben Rice would serve as the DH — a role that almost certainly would have gone to Stanton had he been available — and Goldschmidt will play over at first base. Garcia would then come off the bench as a pinch hitter against righties.
Goldschmidt's overall numbers this season look solid, as he is slashing .253/.316/.455 with 18 home runs and 50 RBI across 370 trips to the dish. Not bad for a 39-year-old.
However, a massive chunk of Goldschmidt's damage was done back in May and June, when he combined for 13 homers and 37 RBI and was a borderline All-Star.
Goldschmidt's production has nose dived since then, but he appears to be kicking it back into gear just in time for the playoffs.
And now that Judge and Stanton are both on the shelf, you can expect Goldschmidt to play a pivotal role.

item.title: [Yanks Go Yard] Brian Cashman foolishly built a Yankees roster that couldn't support Aaron Judge's return
item.dc:creator: Stephen Parello

item.content:encoded:
From June 1 through the August 3 deadline, the New York Yankees were hurting for offense. The club ranked 28th during that span in OPS with a .672 mark. They were 26th in runs scored with 214, an average of 3.96 per game during that 54-game period. The Yankees collectively slashed a putrid .221/.283/.389.
As a result, Brian Cashman went out and bolstered the offense. He acquired Heliot Ramos, who was brutal at the start of his tenure in New York, but has bounced back over the past three weeks. Ramos, though, was an upgrade on the margins as a platoon bat brought into mash lefties. The real get was former Washington Nationals first baseman Luis Garcia Jr.
Garcia Jr. has looked like a budding star, so this next part is tough. He joined an already crowded first base-DH rotation that includes a fringe MVP candidate in Ben Rice and a former MVP who still plays like one against lefties, Paul Goldschmidt, with a 1.006 OPS this season against southpaws.
It made sense, except for one gigantic looming development. The Yankees were expecting to get Aaron Judge back before the end of the season, who would have a much greater impact on New York's offensive output than any external addition could have by a wide margin.
That created a situation that when Judge returned after missing over three months of action, he'd immediately have to jump back in to right field. The Yankees were unable to protect his body and easy him back in at DH thanks to the logjam Cashman created, and as a result, Judge is heading back to the IL after just seven games back. Now, his status for the playoffs is in peril.
Brian Cashman's lack of trade deadline vision put Aaron Judge and the Yankees' World Series hopes at risk
First, a caveat. Judge could have wound up with a calf injury even if he wasn't playing right field. We can get into whether or not he needed more time to ramp up and was brought back too fast, but that's a discussion for another day.
The fact of the matter is that Cashman went out at the deadline and reconstructed the roster in such a way that Judge could only play right field upon his return. That was a mistake.
Now, the market wasn't exactly flush with options, but with some creativity and a willingness to be bold, Cashman could have still completed the necessary task of upgrading the offense while ensuring Judge could be protected by being inserted into the DH spot upon activation.
For example, rather than relying on George Lombard Jr. to man shortstop and provide a spark, he could have gone out and gotten an established young star at the position like Zach Neto or CJ Abrams. Neither player moved at the deadline, but for the right package, they would have. It might have cost Lombard Jr. to get it done, but as we've seen sometimes holding on to even the best prospects can end poorly.
Another lever Cashman could've pulled would've been flexing the franchise's financial might and absorbing Rafael Devers' contract. Yes, Devers just underwent season-ending core muscle surgery, but his blistering .275/.375/.611 second-half performance would have at least bridged the gap until Judge was ready, and perhaps he wouldn't have suffered the same fate had he been dealt here.
Devers has played mostly first base and DH, but while he's not a great third baseman, that's where he has the most experience, and he could've benefited from playing next to the rangy Lombard Jr. Maybe not an ideal solution, but it would've solved the logjam.
Lastly, he could have thought outside the box and beat the Dodgers offer for Tarik Skubal. This wouldn't have helped the offense, but hey, if you struggle to score, you can still win if you make it even harder for your opponent to scratch runs across. In the meantime, the coaching staff could try to figure out why the bats had been so putrid yet hit the third-most homers in MLB (76) during that otherwise horrendous 54-game stretch.
At the end of the day, Cashman did what he always does and went out and got the controllable player with projection over the established star in order to keep his prospect cost down. As a result, he created a logjam that put unnecessary risk on his three-time MVP. If Judge isn't ready in time for the start of October baseball, it will be a devastating blow to the Yankees' World Series aspirations, and it was all completely avoidable.

item.content:encoded:
The final road game of the 2026 regular season is upon us, as the Yankees will conclude it with a seven-game homestand before likely hosting the Red Sox for the Wild Card Series. If the season ends there, this is the end of the line for the gray uniforms for 2026, but obviously, we all hope we'll see them next in Tampa (and more) in early October.
Looking to end a road slate that has been very generous to the Yankees on a high note is Will Warren, who's finishing his sophomore season strong after his great start to the campaign unraveled into a bit of a mess over the summer. Rotation reinforcements that threatened to throw him in the bullpen never came with the recurring injuries, so he'll finish 2026 with 30 starts for the second straight season. This is No. 29, as he enters with a 3.89 ERA (108 ERA+) and 4.07 FIP in 148 innings. No matter what happens from here, Warren has had a successful year in solidifying himself as a true MLB-caliber rotation arm.
Opposing him will be a former Cy Young winner trying to round into form off Tommy John surgery in Corbin Burnes, whom Yankees fans remember well from his lone season in Baltimore in 2024. Returning from a 16-month absence on September 8 to help with the playoff push, Burnes has allowed five runs across 7.2 innings with six strikeouts to two walks against the Royals and Marlins. He isn't totally built up, having thrown 75 pitches in his last start, so expect him to settle around 80-85 today. He's always befuddled the Yankees, pitching to a 1.93 ERA across 23.1 innings in his career, but he doesn't have a win in any of those four starts.
Ben Rice will once again lead off, followed by Cody Bellinger, Heliot Ramos, and Luis García Jr. We've seen better ABs and swings from George Lombard Jr. lately, who'll bat fifth. Spencer Jones is back after a one-day absence due to a sore foot and will bat in front of Anthony Volpe, Austin Wells, and José Caballero.
Lars Nootbaar will also be a repeat leadoff hitter for the D-backs, followed by Ketel Marte, Gabriel Moreno, and Geraldo Perdomo. Corbin Carroll is batting fifth, Nolan Arenado will bat sixth, and former Blue Jay Jesús Sánchez bats seventh ahead of last night's hero Pavin Smith and Tim Tawa.
How to watch
Location: Chase Field, Phoenix, AZ
First pitch: 4:10 pm ET
TV broadcast: YES, DBACKS.TV
Radio broadcast: WFAN 660/101.9 FM, WADO 1280 (NYY), ESPN 620 AM, La Campesina 101.9 FM & 860 AM (AZ)
Online stream: MLB.tv (out-of-market only), Gotham Sports App

item.title: [Pinstripes Nation] La Novia De Anthony Volpe Vuelve A Ser Noticia En Arizona Mientras La Estrella De Los Yankees Se Enfrenta A Los Diamondbacks
item.dc:creator: Inna Zeyger
item.description: PHOENIX — Anthony Volpe tiene muchas cosas en las que centrarse ahora que los Yankees se preparan para octubre. Su novia, Elle Jowett, por su parte, ha encontrado un rincón mucho más tranquilo de Arizona. Jowett volvió a ser tema de conversación fuera del campo entre los Yankees el domingo, después de compartir unas fotos de una excursión por el sendero Cathedral Rock Trail, en Sedona, mientras Volpe y el equipo de Nueva York estaban en el estado para disputar su serie de tres partidos contra lo
item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Anthony Volpe tiene muchas cosas en las que centrarse ahora que los Yankees se preparan para octubre. Su novia, Elle Jowett, por su parte, ha encontrado un rincón mucho más tranquilo de Arizona.
Jowett volvió a ser tema de conversación fuera del campo entre los Yankees el domingo, después de compartir unas fotos de una excursión por el sendero Cathedral Rock Trail, en Sedona, mientras Volpe y el equipo de Nueva York estaban en el estado para disputar su serie de tres partidos contra los Diamondbacks de Arizona.
La modelo, afincada en Nueva York, se fue de excursión a Cathedral Rock y compartió unas fotos en las que aparece meditando en el sendero. Jowett llevaba una camiseta deportiva y unos leggings mientras posaba con el característico paisaje de rocas rojas y el entorno desértico de Sedona de fondo.
El momento hace que una publicación sobre un estilo de vida que, por lo demás, sería muy sencilla, adquiera un toque relacionado con los Yankees.
Mientras Jowett disfrutaba del paisaje de Arizona, Volpe seguía inmerso en una aventura de septiembre muy diferente, a unos 190 kilómetros de distancia, en Phoenix.
Jowett sale a la luz durante una racha importante de los Yankees
Los Yankees ya se han asegurado su participación en el béisbol de octubre, tras conseguir su tercera clasificación consecutiva para la postemporada. Lo que aún está por decidir es su recorrido en la postemporada.
El sábado nos volvió a recordar que los partidos que quedan no son para tomárselos a la ligera.
Arizona venció a Nueva York por 5-3 gracias a un jonrón de dos carreras de Pavin Smith en la novena entrada que dio la victoria a su equipo. Con esta derrota, los Yankees quedan con un balance de 89-65, lo que les mantiene bajo presión en la recta final de la temporada regular.
Volpe participó de lleno en el ataque de Nueva York.
Jugó como segunda base, conectó 1 de 4, bateó un sencillo en la quinta entrada y luego anotó la primera carrera de los Yankees gracias a un fly de sacrificio de Ben Rice.
Esto convierte a la serie en otra buena prueba de fuego de octubre para un equipo de los Yankees que ya tiene asegurada su participación más allá de la temporada regular.
El papel de Volpe en los Yankees ha cambiado radicalmente
El puesto de Volpe en la alineación se ha convertido en uno de los temas más interesantes que rodean al equipo.
Los Yankees lo bajaron a la Triple A durante la segunda mitad de la temporada tras sus problemas ofensivos. Durante su etapa en las ligas menores, Volpe empezó a jugar de segunda base, alejándose de la posición de campocorto que definió sus primeros años en las Grandes Ligas.
Más tarde, Nueva York lo volvió a llamar después de que la lesión en el pulgar de Jazz Chisholm Jr. dejara un hueco en el cuadro.
Volpe anunció su regreso a lo grande el 10 de septiembre, con una actuación de tres hits y cinco carreras impulsadas, que incluyó un grand slam en la victoria de los Yankees por 10-3 sobre Colorado. Después admitió que nada de lo relacionado con su regreso estaba garantizado cuando Nueva York lo envió inicialmente a la Triple A.
Volpe está aprovechando al máximo su segunda oportunidad con los Yankees
Y lo que es más importante para los Yankees, Volpe no ha dejado que ese memorable partido de regreso sea un caso aislado.
En sus últimos ocho partidos hasta el domingo, este jugador de 25 años tenía un promedio de bateo de .296, con un porcentaje de embasado de .345 y un porcentaje de slugging de .481, lo que le da un OPS de .826. Consiguió ocho hits en 27 turnos al bate durante ese periodo, incluyendo dos dobles y un jonrón, además de impulsar siete carreras.
Esas cifras suponen una respuesta significativa por parte de un jugador cuyo futuro en los Yankees parecía mucho menos seguro cuando el club lo envió de vuelta a la Triple A.
El regreso de Volpe también vino acompañado de un cambio de posición. En lugar de recuperar inmediatamente el puesto de campocorto, ha estado jugando en segunda base mientras los Yankees evalúan cómo podría encajar su cuadro interior en octubre.
Este experimento ha añadido otra dimensión a su resurgimiento de final de temporada.
No consiguió ningún hit en sus cuatro turnos al bate durante la victoria del viernes por 9-2 contra Arizona, pero el sábado respondió con un sencillo y una carrera anotada.
La tendencia general sigue siendo alentadora.
Volpe llegó a esta recta final con la necesidad de demostrar que su paso por la Triple A había dado frutos tangibles. En lugar de volver simplemente porque una lesión le había dejado un hueco, ha empezado a dar a los Yankees motivos para seguir dándole oportunidades al bate.
Eso podría ser muy importante cuando el entrenador Aaron Boone empiece a decidir qué combinación de infield le da a Nueva York su mejor alineación para la postemporada.
Elle Jowett ha ido acaparando cada vez más la atención de los Yankees
La aparición de Jowett en Arizona no es la primera vez que su actividad en las redes sociales llama la atención en un momento importante de la temporada de Volpe.
Ella y Volpe se hicieron públicos como pareja durante la temporada de 2025 tras aparecer juntos en la gala Willow Grant de la Fundación Carlos Rodón en Greenwich, Connecticut.
Posteriormente, Jowett asistió a partidos de la postemporada de los Yankees, aunque la pareja ha mantenido en general su relación al margen de sus propias redes sociales.
A principios de este año, Jowett volvió a aparecer en los titulares tras compartir fotos de Los Ángeles más o menos cuando los Yankees enviaron a Volpe a la Triple A. Otros miembros de la gran familia de los Yankees interactuaron con esa publicación.
Más tarde, llamó la atención con otra publicación de modelaje coincidiendo con el regreso de Volpe a las Grandes Ligas.
Ahora, Arizona es el último punto de encuentro entre los mundos separados de la pareja.
El fin de semana de Jowett ha girado en torno a la meditación y al paisaje de rocas rojas de Sedona. El de Volpe, por su parte, ha estado marcado por un equipo de los Yankees , que se dirige a la postemporada, que ha tenido que lidiar con una derrota en la última entrada, un panorama cambiante en el cuadro y decisiones cada vez más importantes sobre su alineación para octubre.
Los contextos no podrían ser más diferentes.
Pero ahora que octubre está a la vuelta de la esquina, ambas han vuelto a poner la vida fuera del campo de Volpe al mismo nivel que uno de los tramos más decisivos de su temporada con los Yankees.
¿Qué le parece? Deje su comentario a continuación.

item.content:encoded:
Nueva York, Nueva York.- Cody Bellinger conectó dos jonrones de dos carreras, impulsó cinco carreras y los Yankees de Nueva York aplastaron a los Reales de Kansas City por 13-4 el sábado por la tarde.
El abridor de Nueva York, Will Warren (2-0), igualó su récord personal con 11 ponches y lanzó un juego de dos carreras en siete entradas.
Bellinger conectó un jonrón de dos carreras durante una entrada de cinco carreras en la tercera entrada contra Noah Cameron (1-1) y llevó a Nueva York a su victoria más abultada de la temporada. Bellinger conectó un jonrón de dos carreras contra Mitch Spence en la sexta entrada, después de haber impulsado una carrera con un sencillo en la cuarta.
Bellinger logró su vigésimo partido con múltiples jonrones de su carrera y los Yankees conectaron cuatro jonrones por segunda vez en la temporada.
Bellinger conectó su primer jonrón entre un batazo de dos carreras de Amed Rosario y un jonrón solitario de Ben Rice, aprovechando los Yankees un error de tres bases del jardinero central Kyle Isbel en un elevado de JC Escarra.
Isbel le arrebató la pelota del guante al jardinero derecho Jac Caglianone cuando ambos se encontraban cerca de la zona de advertencia, y los Yankees respondieron con su demostración de poder contra el lanzador zurdo.
Rosario, abriendo el orden al bate por segunda vez en la temporada, envió un lanzamiento cortado a las gradas del jardín derecho. Tras una base por bolas de Aaron Judge, Bellinger conectó un slider en el primer lanzamiento que llegó al segundo piso del jardín derecho, poniendo el marcador 4-0 a favor de su equipo.
Dos bateadores después, Rice conectó un jonrón por tercer partido consecutivo al mandar la bola rápida de Cameron a las gradas del jardín derecho.
Escarra conectó un doble productor y un triple de dos carreras en la séptima entrada. Rosario también impulsó una carrera con un sencillo antes de que Bellinger volviera a conectar. Randal Grichuk impulsó su primera carrera como Yankee con un elevado de sacrificio en las últimas entradas.
Cameron fue castigado con siete carreras, la mayor cantidad en su carrera (cinco limpias), y siete hits en cuatro entradas.
Carter Jensen conectó un jonrón de dos carreras en la séptima entrada, pero los Royals sufrieron su sexta derrota consecutiva y la novena en 11 partidos. Kansas City también perdió su décimo partido consecutivo contra los Yankees desde el segundo juego de la Serie Divisional de la Liga Americana de 2024.
Antes de que Cameron hiciera su primer lanzamiento, el mánager de los Royals, Matt Quatraro, fue expulsado por el árbitro de segunda base, Nestor Ceja.
A continuación
El lanzador zurdo de Kansas City, Cole Ragans (0-3, 3.78 ERA), se enfrenta al lanzador zurdo de Nueva York, Ryan Weathers (0-2, 4.29), en el último partido de la serie del domingo.
Información: AP.

item.title: [Sports Illustrated] What the Yankees' Lineup Should Look Like Without Aaron Judge In October
item.dc:creator: Michael Zeno; Unknown
item.description: Aaron Judge's regular season may be over, but that doesn't mean the Yankees' has to be. item.content:encoded:
Aaron Judge's regular season may be over, but that doesn't mean the Yankees' has to be.
A mystery calf ailment popped up suddenly on Wednesday and has resulted in the Yankees captain being placed on the injured list. It's unclear whether he will return in 2026, even if he's eligible to return next weekend. Aaron Boone did not give any information on the severity of the calf issue, but the timeline is likely not good due to how tricky those injuries prove to be.
A scenario is now potentially unfolding that would have only appeared in Boone's nightmares: a postseason without the best hitter in baseball, with a lineup that struggled mightily without him. Even if they seemed to gradually improve as time went on, particularly in August, it would be a massive blow if he cannot return.
You can't replace a guy like Judge midseason; you can merely do your best to make up for his absence. Fortunately, on a platoon-heavy team like this, they should have plenty of options to build a lineup without him for the playoffs.
What the playoff lineup should look like against right-handed pitching
- Ben Rice (DH)
- Cody Bellinger (LF)
- Luis García Jr. (1B)
- Heliot Ramos (RF)
- Spencer Jones (CF)
- Jazz Chisholm Jr. (2B)
- George Lombard Jr. (SS)
- Austin Wells (C)
- Ryan McMahon (3B)
This lineup simultaneously features the easiest decisions, but also the roughest circumstances. Having a guy like Judge as the ultimate lineup balancer who mashed both lefties and righties allowed you to use plenty of left-handed hitters at the top of the order, something that the team has in abundance.
The best right-handed hitter on the roster without Judge is hard to pinpoint, especially since all of them are significantly worse against same-handed pitching. Heliot Ramos might just be the best option to bat highest among them, which would be cleanup in this scenario.
It's not an ideal situation in the slightest. Even if you don't think it makes sense to bat Ramos that high because of his struggles against righties, there is some merit to breaking up the team's many left-handed bats. In a lineup that will likely only feature one other righty, it has to be considered.
The fate of this lineup when they're out there, which would likely be mostly after a potential Wild Card Series with the Red Sox, would hinge on the middle. Spencer Jones and Jazz Chisholm Jr. got hot in August and helped the offensive turnaround begin, but both are heavily streaky bats with contact issues. If they go cold, this lineup might limp through games like they did in July.
What the playoff lineup should look like against left-handed pitching
- Paul Goldschmidt (1B)
- Cody Bellinger (LF)
- Heliot Ramos (RF)
- Ben Rice (DH)
- George Lombard Jr. (SS)
- Spencer Jones (CF)
- Jazz Chisholm Jr. (2B)
- Anthony Volpe/José Caballero (3B)
- Austin Wells (C)
Here's where it gets interesting. How far do you lean into the platoons on a team with several players designated to specifically hit lefties, especially against a team that will likely lean heavily on those types of pitchers in Boston?
Many Yankees fans believe that it would be improper to take a guy like García, who is likely the team's second-best pound-for-pound hitter with Judge injured, out of the lineup, but you don't really have a choice here. He's slashing just .238/.274/.363 against lefties, while Goldschmidt has been among the team's best hitters against them for the last two seasons. Add in Rice's improvements against same-handed pitching, and it just needs to be done.
Using him in a different position is also just not happening. He has not played second base, where he was extremely poor, since 2025. The only position he's played this season is first base. If he wasn't so dreadful out there, maybe he could replace Chisholm, a mediocre hitter against lefties in his own right.
Speaking of defense, you might notice the lack of Amed Rosario, and that's intentional. Rosario's use on this roster was almost exclusively predicated on his ability to hit left-handed pitching, but he's been significantly worse at it this season. Add in his truly dreadful defense, and you have a conundrum.
Anthony Volpe is a better hitter than José Caballero, but there are questions about how his arm strength would play at third, where he's also very inexperienced with just three games played in Triple-A. Caballero would probably get the nod here, but he's someone who just plays better off the bench with his speed and versatility.
It's also an aggressive placement for Lombard, batting fifth in his first career playoff game. The results haven't quite been there yet for him, but he's always been significantly better against lefties and should be slid up the lineup and be treated as one of those platoon bats who are there to hit that handedness, even if it might lead to consequences in the bullpen.
Boston is loaded with left-handed pitching from the rotation to the bullpen, so there will be few opportunities to get to a guy like García on the bench. The rest of the bench would be situational with pinch runners and pinch hitters.
Things ultimately look particularly shallow, but is there a chance that some last-minute reinforcements could help out?
Could Trent Grisham or Giancarlo Stanton return to provide relief?
It seems unlikely, especially early in the postseason, but the Yankees are refusing to shut the door on either Trent Grisham's or Giancarlo Stanton's return.
Grisham, who suffered a Grade 2 hamstring strain earlier this month, was revealed to be "pretty far along" in his running program, and Boone said it's not out of the question that he returns in the season's final days, although an exact timeline for that has not been spelled out. If Grisham is physically ready to get back on the field, it would provide a boost, even if he might not be starting over Jones at this point.
Stanton, who's been out since April due to two separate calf strains and a re-aggravation, has continued to hit through his rehab, but hasn't resumed running as of last Sunday. Considering how it took several weeks for him to even get close to back from injury with his running program last time, this likely doesn't put him in play until the ALCS at the earliest.
While Stanton seems significantly less likely to get into a game again this season, there is a path for Grisham. The team could use him and Ramos in a platoon situation to add yet another lefty to the lineup against right-handed pitching. They could also utilize him as a pinch hitter on a larger bench than usual, due to the team's propensity to carry fewer than 13 pitchers in the Wild Card Series.
The real question for Grisham is defensive. While Jones has absolutely looked shaky in center field, the struggles of Grisham out there are well documented. Add in his diminished athleticism and likely balky hamstring straight off an injury, would it be better if the team just chanced it by throwing him in right field when he plays?
He hasn't played the position since a disastrous error lost the Brewers the 2019 Wild Card Game against the Nationals, but playing it at Yankee Stadium is significantly easier than dealing with the spacious center field. Of course, this is something the Yankees would have to determine their willingness to do beforehand and have him practice the position, so what plans they have will be determined by that.
As for Stanton if he's ever medically able to get back? There just might not be any room for him with Rice as the permanent DH. You don't want to take the bat out of either of their hands, and with the team seemingly having to juggle multiple guys coming off soft-tissue injuries, can they afford to use a roster spot for a designated pinch hitter as they did with 2022 Matt Carpenter?

item.dc:creator: Esteban Quiñones

item.content:encoded:
PHOENIX — Los Yankees se pasaron casi toda la noche del sábado lidiando con dos realidades en el Chase Field. Cam Schlittler volvió a ofrecerles una gran salida, pero cada entrada cobró más importancia después de que Tampa Bay ya se hubiera llevado la victoria con un tanto decisivo en la última entrada.
Nueva York tuvo la oportunidad de evitar que sus cada vez más remotas opciones en la División Este de la Liga Americana se le escaparan aún más. En cambio, los Yankees se fueron con una derrota por 5-3 ante los Diamondbacks de Arizona, lo que amplió su desventaja en la división a cinco partidos cuando solo quedan ocho por disputar.
Los Yankees hicieron lo suficiente para que el partido se pudiera ganar. Ben Rice conectó un fly de sacrificio en la quinta entrada. Heliot Ramos y Austin Wells conectaron jonrones en la sexta. Schlittler superó su primer bajón serio en el control en semanas y terminó seis entradas concediendo solo una carrera limpia.
Arizona siguió respondiendo. Jordan Lawlar neutralizó la primera ventaja de Nueva York con un triple de dos carreras en la quinta entrada, después de que Schlittler fallara al intentar atrapar un toque. Corbin Carroll empató el partido con un fly de sacrificio en la sexta entrada, tras dos bases por bolas y un sencillo de toque que llenaron las bases.
Lo que estaba en juego ya estaba claro antes del primer lanzamiento. Varios jugadores de los Yankees vieron desde el vestuario de visitantes cómo Tampa Bay vencía a Boston por 2-1, un resultado que situaba a los Rays cinco partidos por delante. Nueva York había ganado ocho de sus últimos diez partidos, pero la racha de Tampa Bay casi no dejaba margen para perder otra oportunidad.
A continuación, los Yankees contaron con dos entradas sin puntos de su bullpen. Brent Headrick consiguió dos outs en la séptima antes de que Paul Blackburn terminara esa entrada y se encargara de la octava. El marcador se mantuvo en 3-3, lo que dejaba a Nueva York a una entrada limpia de tener otra oportunidad al bate.
Schlittler había hecho lo suficiente para mantener a los Yankees en el partido. Cedió tres hits y tres carreras, solo una limpia, y se anotó seis strikeouts en 98 lanzamientos. Su promedio de carreras limpias bajó a 1,94. Para entonces, el margen de error era ya casi nulo.
Fue entonces cuando el partido dio un giro con la decisión más decisiva de Aaron Boone de toda la noche respecto al bullpen.
Boone recurre a Fulmer con el partido en juego
Boone le pasó la parte baja de la novena a Michael Fulmer en lugar de al cerrador David Bednar. Fulmer había lanzado dos tercios de una entrada sin encajar carreras en la victoria del viernes por 9-2, mientras que Bednar no había lanzado desde que hizo dos entradas el miércoles en Minnesota.
Fulmer parecía haber eliminado a Ildemaro Vargas con un strikeout en un lanzamiento con cuenta completa, pero Vargas impugnó la decisión a través del sistema automático de bolas y strikes de la MLB. El lanzamiento se consideró bola, lo que le dio a Arizona una base por bolas para abrir el turno.
Fulmer ponchó a Lawlar. A continuación, Pavin Smith entró como bateador suplente y mandó el segundo lanzamiento de Fulmer, un «cutter», 391 pies al campo derecho para un jonrón de dos carreras que dio la victoria.
Juan Morillo se llevó la victoria para Arizona, mejorando su balance a 5-4. Fulmer sufrió su primera derrota y vio cómo su promedio de carreras limpias subía de 1,59 a 3,09. No hubo salvamento.
La decisión llamó la atención porque Bednar llegaba a la noche con 34 salvamentos y una efectividad de 2,58. Fulmer, fichado por los Yankees a finales de agosto, solo había lanzado 11 1/3 entradas en las Grandes Ligas esta temporada antes del sábado y sigue formando parte de un bullpen muy concurrido de la postemporada.
Schlittler asume la culpa tras una racha irregular
Un error de Schlittler en la quinta entrada ayudó a Arizona a anotar dos veces, y ocho lanzamientos seguidos fuera de la zona al inicio de la sexta propiciaron la remontada que empató el partido. Se recuperó ponchando a Nolan Arenado y a Tim Tawa con dos corredores en posición de anotar.
El lanzador diestro se centró en su propio error tras el partido.
«Asumo toda la culpa por eso», dijo Schlittler. «Cometí un error ahí y dejé que nos marcaran dos carreras. Así es el béisbol, pero esa la tengo yo».
Schlittler ha cedido una carrera limpia o menos en 24 salidas como titular, lo que le convierte, junto a Sandy Koufax y Bob Gibson, en uno de los únicos lanzadores de la Era de la Bola Viva con al menos 24 salidas de este tipo en una temporada, sin contar los «openers».
El descanso de Bednar acentúa el contraste en el bullpen
La secuencia de relevos de los Yankees ofreció un anticipo de la postemporada. Headrick y Blackburn sumaron entre ambos dos entradas sin encajar carreras antes de la novena. Bednar no llegó a salir, mientras que Fulmer lanzó dos días seguidos.
Fulmer llegaba al sábado con una ERA de 1,59 y había limitado a sus rivales a un promedio de bateo de 0,171 en sus apariciones con los Yankees. La diferencia en la carga de trabajo era aún más marcada: Fulmer había lanzado el viernes, mientras que Bednar había tenido dos días completos de descanso tras su salida de dos entradas del miércoles.
Esto es importante ahora que los Yankees están reorganizando una plantilla de lanzadores que se reducirá de cara a octubre. Bednar es una opción consolidada para las últimas entradas. Fulmer ha lanzado lo suficientemente bien como para seguir en la pugna por un puesto en la plantilla, pero su puesto está menos asegurado, ya que varios relevistas compiten por las limitadas plazas de la postemporada.
El sábado supuso otro momento de evaluación, y esta vez se dio en un momento de máxima presión.
Los Yankees pierden más terreno antes del enfrentamiento con los Rays
Con esta derrota, los Yankees se quedan con un balance de 89-65. Tampa Bay sube a 94-60, lo que deja a Nueva York a cinco partidos de distancia en la División Este de la Liga Americana. Los Yankees siguen teniendo una ventaja de 5 partidos y medio sobre Boston en la lucha por el primer puesto de comodín de la Liga Americana.
Boone reconoció lo estrecho que se ha vuelto el camino con cuatro partidos contra Tampa Bay a partir del martes en el Yankee Stadium.
«Si les barreríamos, entonces la cosa se pondría interesante», dijo Boone. «Pero no puedes barrerlos antes del partido [del domingo]».
Los Yankees cierran la serie contra Arizona el domingo, con Will Warren como lanzador previsto para enfrentarse a Corbin Burnes. Tras el partido del sábado, Nueva York debe mantener viva la lucha por el título de división y, al mismo tiempo, decidir en qué relevos confía Boone cuando llegue la próxima novena entrada empatada.
¿Qué opinas? Deja tu comentario aquí abajo.
